Mitigating the Curse of Detail: Scaling Arguments for Feature Learning and Sample Complexity

Noa Rubin Affiliation: Racah Institute of Physics
Hebrew University
Jerusalem, Israel    Orit Davidovich Affiliation: IBM Research
Haifa, Israel.    Zohar Ringel Affiliation: Racah Institute of Physics
Hebrew University
Jerusalem, Israel
Abstract

Two pressing topics in the theory of deep learning are the interpretation of feature learning (FL) mechanisms and the determination of implicit bias of networks in the rich regime. Current theories of rich FL often appear in the form of high-dimensional non-linear equations, which require computationally intensive numerical solutions. Given the many details that go into defining a deep learning problem, this analytical complexity is a significant and often unavoidable challenge. Here, we propose a powerful heuristic route for predicting the data and width scales at which various patterns of FL emerge. This form of scale analysis is considerably simpler than such exact theories and reproduces the scaling exponents of various known results. In addition, we make novel predictions on complex toy architectures, such as three-layer non-linear networks and attention heads, thus extending the scope of first-principle theories of deep learning.

1 Introduction

There is a clear need for a better theoretical understanding of deep learning. However, efforts to construct such theories inevitably suffer from a “curse of details”. Indeed, since any choice of architecture, activation, data measure, and training protocol affects performance, finding a theory with true predictive power that accurately accounts for all those details is unlikely. One workaround is to focus on analytically tractable toy models, an approach that can often uncover interesting fundamental aspects. However, analytical tractability is a fragile, fine-tuned property; thus, a large explainability gap remains between such toy models and more complex data/architecture settings.

An alternative approach focuses on scaling properties of neural networks, which appear more robust. Two well-established examples are empirically predicting network performance by extrapolating learning curves using power laws kaplan2020scaling; hestness2017deeplearningscalingpredictable, and providing theory-inspired suggestions for hyperparameter transfer techniques yang2022tensorprogramsvtuning; bordelon2023depthwise. Indeed, it is often the case cardy1996scaling that predicting scaling exponents is easier than predicting exact or approximate behaviors. As a simple toy model of this, consider the integral ∫−∞∞d​x​g​(x/P)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dxg(x/P). While g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) needs to be fine-tuned for exact computations, a change of variable reveals a robust linear scaling with PP for any g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot).

This work focuses on scaling properties of feature learning (FL). This phenomenon, and, more generally, interpretability, has been studied extensively both from the practical and theoretical sides. On the practical side, mechanistic interpretability bereska2024mechanisticinterpretabilityaisafety has provided us with statistical explanations for why some predictions are made and the underlying decision mechanisms. On the theory side, kernel approaches bordelon2022self; aitchison2021deep Saad and Solla type approaches Saad1995; Bruno2023; bietti2022learning (and their Bayesian counterparts cui2025highdimensionallearningnarrowneural) allow us to solve simple non-linear teacher-student networks in the rich regime.

This work examines feature learning through a Bayesian lens, where it is often defined as a deviation from the Gaussian Process (GP) prior. This deviation has been shown to manifest in several distinct regime dependent ways, including: (i) updates to the kernel while the distribution remains Gaussian LiSompolinsky2021; rubin_kernels_2025; ariosto2022statistical; seroussi2023separation; aitchison2019bigger; (ii) the distribution changes from zero mean-Gaussian to a mixture of Gaussians rubin_grokking_2024; and (iii) the specialization of specific neurons barbier_statistical_2025; as well as combinations of the above ringel_applications_2025; meegen_coding_2024. However, the frameworks capturing these FL effects are often mathematically cumbersome and restricted to shallow networks. Even when extended to deep architectures barbier_statistical_2025; li2020statistical, their computational complexity prevents the derivation of intuitive scaling laws. Ultimately, this difficulty in computation compounds with the context-specificity of these mechanisms, complicating unified comparison of scaling laws across varied architectural settings.

In this work, we introduce a novel heuristic framework addressing the challenging task of making first-principles predictions on sample complexity and feature learning effects in Bayesian NNs. We consider Bayesian NNs as these are a standard proxy for SGD-trained networks at equilibrium mingard2020sgd; mandt2017stochastic. The heuristic nature of our approach (see Fig. 1 for a schematic overview), allows us to bypass otherwise highly complex analysis and extract insights using simple pen-and-paper calculations, resulting in non-trivial predictions across a broad range of architectures and settings. We indeed validate our framework for two- and three-layer fully connected networks (using ReLU and Erf activations), attention heads, and convolutional neural networks, covering both teacher-student, regression, and classification tasks. Across these diverse settings, our main results are:

  1. 1.

    Predicting feature learning patterns: We predict which of the FL phenomena from the literature discussed above will emerge in different architectures and across varying scales of architectural variables, such as input dimension, layer width, regularization, and parametrization choices such as mean-field versus standard scaling. We map transitions between these patterns and derive the explicit scaling laws governing their strength.

  2. 2.

    Predicting sample complexity scale: We determine the scaling behavior of P∗P_{*}, the threshold sample size at which learning is possible, as a function of the architectural variables and parametrization choices.

2 Setup

We consider here several types of feedforward networks, but, for the sake of clarity, we illustrate the main derivation on deep fully connected networks (FCNs) and, later, when we analyze specific problems, augment it for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) as needed. Our FCNs are defined by

f⁡(x)=∑i=1NL−1wiL​σ​(hiL−1​(x)),wherehil>1​(x)=∑j=1Nl−1Wi​jl​σ​(hjl−1​(x)),hj1​(x)=∑k=1dWj​k1​xk,\displaystyle f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{L-1}}w^{L}_{i}\sigma(h_{i}^{L-1}(x)),\quad\text{where}\ \ h_{i}^{l>1}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{l-1}}W_{ij}^{l}\sigma(h_{j}^{l-1}(x)),\ \ h_{j}^{1}(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}W_{jk}^{1}x_{k}, (1)

where σ\sigma can be any activation function, and we refer to hilh^{l}_{i}’s as pre-acitvations. We consider Bayesian neural networks, as Bayesian descriptions are a commonly used proxy for network behavior after long-time stochastic training wilson_bayesian_2020; wilson_case_2020; naveh2021predicting. Alternatively, they represent an exact solution to Langevin dynamics with weight decay welling_bayesian_nodate. We denote the target function by yy and the training sample size by PP, and assume training with Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. The quadratic weight decay for each layer ll is set to κ​Nl−1/σl2\kappa N_{l-1}/\sigma_{l}^{2}, where κ\kappa is the ridge parameter and N0=dN_{0}=d is the input dimension. This choice of weight decay results in a Gaussian prior distribution for the weights given by Wi,jl∼𝒩⁡(0,σl2/Nl−1)W_{i,j}^{l}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{l}^{2}/N_{l-1}) for i=1,..,Nli=1,..,N_{l} , j=1,…,Nl−1j=1,...,N_{l-1}. The possible outputs ff of such a network, given yy and PP, are then distributed according to the posterior:

π(f∣y,P)=1Zexp(−12​κ∑ν=1P[f(xν)−y(xν)]2)p0(f),\pi\left(f\mid y,P\right)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\kappa}\sum_{\nu=1}^{P}\left[f(x_{\nu})-y(x_{\nu})\right]^{2}\right)p_{0}(f), (2)

where ZZ is the normalization constant, {xν}ν=1P\{x_{\nu}\}_{\nu=1}^{P} is the training dataset of size PP, and p0​(f)p_{0}(f) is the prior defined as p0​(f)=∫d​Θ​p​(Θ)​δ​[f−fΘ]p_{0}(f)=\int d\Theta p\left(\Theta\right)\delta\left[f-f_{\Theta}\right], determined by the weight decay. Here, Θ\Theta is the collection of all network weights, and p⁡(Θ)p\left(\Theta\right) corresponds to the density of the prior weight distribution, which we take to be Gaussian with a diagonal covariance, representing quadratic weight decay, and fΘf_{\Theta} is the network architecture with weights Θ\Theta. We further set p⁡(Θ)p(\Theta) such that pre-activations are all 𝒪⁡(1){\mathcal{O}}(1) under the prior He2015. For classification tasks, see App. A.2. As a measure for learning, we consider an observable, which we refer to as alignment, given by

Af:=⟨f,y⟩/⟨y,y⟩,A_{f}:=\langle f,y\rangle/\langle y,y\rangle, (3)

where ⟨g,h⟩=∫d​μx​g​(x)​h​(x)\langle g,h\rangle=\int d\mu_{x}g(x)h(x) is the functional inner product, and d​μxd\mu_{x} is some test measure, which, conveniently, does not need to be the measure from which the training set was drawn. We similarly define ⟨g,K,h⟩=∫d​μx​d​μx′​g​(x)​K​(x,x′)​h​(x′)\langle g,K,h\rangle=\int d\mu_{x}d\mu_{x^{\prime}}g(x)K(x,x^{\prime})h(x^{\prime}) for any kernel KK. Alignment represents the extent to which the network learns a function that is proportional to the target. It bounds the test MSE via the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ∫d​μx​(f⁡(x)−y⁡(x))2≥⟨y,y⟩​(Af−1)2\int d\mu_{x}(f(x)-y(x))^{2}\geq\langle y,y\rangle(A_{f}-1)^{2}. Having Af≈1A_{f}\approx 1 is thus a necessary condition for successful learning.

3 Alignment and Sample Complexity

We turn to analyze sample complexity via an upper bound on the probability of finding Af≥αA_{f}\geq\alpha for α≈1\alpha\approx 1. We begin with a theoretical bound on the posterior that mainly depends on the chance that a random network, chosen from the prior, produces an alignment of at least α\alpha. We denote the prior and posterior alignment probabilities by Prp0[Af≥α]\Pr_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right] and Prπ[Af≥α]\Pr_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right] respectively. Following simple arguments (see App. A and App. A.2 for generalization to classification.), we obtain the following bound on the log posterior 11 1 See also lavie_demystifying_2025, for a similar data-agnostic bound in the context of lazy learning.

log(Prπ[Af≥α])<Pk/(2κ)+log(Prp0[Af≥α]),\log\left(\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\right)<Pk/\left(2\kappa\right)+\log\left(\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\right), (4)

where k=P−1​∑ν=1P𝔼p0​[(f⁡(xν)−y⁡(xν))2]k=P^{-1}\sum_{\nu=1}^{P}\mathbb{E}_{p_{0}}[(f(x_{\nu})-y(x_{\nu}))^{2}] is the only training-set dependent quantity and is generally of order one. The Bayesian interpretation of successful learning is having Prπ[Af≥α]≈𝒪(1)\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\approx{\mathcal{O}}(1). 22 2 More concretely, we can assume some tolerance ϵ\epsilon and then π⁡(Af≈1)=(ϵ)−1​∫0ϵd​ϵ​π​(Af=1−ϵ)\pi\left(A_{f}\approx 1\right)=(\epsilon)^{-1}\int_{0}^{\epsilon}d\epsilon\pi(A_{f}=1-\epsilon). Since a random network is unlikely to achieve strong alignment, logPrp0[Af≥α]\log\Pr_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right] would typically be highly negative for large α\alpha. Therefore, a sufficiently large data term is required to cancel this effect. Explicitly,

P≳−2κlogPrp0[Af≥α]/k.\displaystyle P\gtrsim-2\kappa\log\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]/k. (5)

Thus, up to the ridge parameter and the 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) factor kk, depending on the training set, the log probability of prior alignment with the target lower bounds the sample complexity. Here, it is worth noting that the bound becomes tight when overfitting effects are small, which is typically the case for k/κ∼𝒪⁡(1)k/\kappa\sim\mathcal{O}(1). Taking κ→0\kappa\rightarrow 0 encourages overfitting (though often benignly bartlett_benign_2020) and trivializes this bound. We conjecture that, in this case, κ\kappa should be kept 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) based on the effective ridge treatment canatar_spectral_2021; cohen_learning_2021; bartlett_benign_2020. Establishing this conjecture is outside the scope of this work. From a PAC-Bayesian perspective, an analogous bound would require PP to be much larger than the KL-divergence between the prior and posterior33 3 Following the data-processing-inequality, one can lower-bound the KL-divergence between the full prior and posterior probabilities by the KL-divergence of a coarser probability of an Af≥αA_{f}\geq\alpha event in the prior and posterior. The latter KL divergence is given by −logPrp0[Af≥α]-\log\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right] (e.g., 10.1145/307400.307435). More recently, prior-posterior relations have been studied in the context of complex Boolean functions mingard2025characterisinginductivebiasesneural.

Following the Chernoff inequality, we can find an upper bound for the probability (and a lower bound for PP) via

P≥−2κ/klogPrp0[Af≥α]≥2κ/kE(α),E(α)=−loginft>0e−t​α𝔼p0[et​Af].P\geq-2\kappa/k\ \log\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\geq 2\kappa/k\ E(\alpha),\ \ \ E(\alpha)=-\log\inf_{t>0}e^{-t\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{p_{0}}\left[e^{tA_{f}}\right]. (6)

Where we refer to E⁡(α)E(\alpha) as the energy. We can thus express the minimal sample size necessary for learning, P∗P_{*}, through the energy as P∗∝E⁡(α)P_{*}\propto E(\alpha). In App. B, we provide an asymptotically exact solution for E⁡(α)E(\alpha), and compute it explicitly for a two layer network. We also argue and demonstrate that our bound is inherently tied to FL. Indeed, a network sampled from the prior that achieves such alignment is a statistical outlier, driven by the emergence of an internal structure which mimics FL (see also Fig. 2). Nevertheless, such a direct LDT approach is computationally prohibitive in most cases of interest. We therefore introduce a heuristic LDT-based method for evaluating P∗P_{*}. This method not only enables predicting the scaling of P∗P_{*} but also the FL effects that lead to successful learning.

In this section, we adopt a variational approach to estimating P∗P_{*} by comparing different modes of feature learning 44 4 Viewed here formally as emergent weight/pre-activation structures enabling the outlier. under a certain loss (see (11) below). While many approaches predict different FL mechanisms pacelli_statistical_2023; fischer_critical_2024; meegen_coding_2024; buzaglo_how_2025; LiSompolinsky2021; seroussi_separation_2023; rubin_kernels_2025; rubin_grokking_2024; barbier_statistical_2025, they are often case-dependent, highly detailed, and complex. Thus, we propose a method that abstracts key FL mechanisms from these frameworks into distinct, comparable patterns.

4 Variational Analysis

Our next objective is to make the sample complexity bound tractable. This requires estimating the prior probability term, Prp0[Af≥α]\Pr_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right], for alignments α≈1\alpha\approx 1. As a first step, we simplify this by relating the cumulative distribution function to the probability density denoted by pAf​(α)p_{A_{f}}(\alpha). As shown in App. A.3, for large alignments, we have E⁡(α)≈−log⁡pAf​(α)E(\alpha)\approx-\log p_{A_{f}}(\alpha). This allows us to re-express P∗P_{*} in terms of the density: P∗=−2κlogpAf(α)/kP_{*}=-2\kappa\log p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)/k. However, computing pAf​(α)p_{A_{f}}(\alpha) directly remains intractable. We therefore turn to a variational approach to estimate it. As explained in the next section, we wish to express the variational probability density in terms of pre-activations hh (1). Accordingly, in App. C.1, we follow standard statistical mechanics techniques to express this density as

pAf​(α)=∫𝒟​h​𝒩​(α∣0,⟨y,K~L−1,y⟩)​∏l=1L−1∏i=1Nl𝒩⁡(hil∣0,K~l−1)\displaystyle p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)=\int\mathcal{D}h\,\mathcal{N}\left(\alpha\mid 0,\langle y,\tilde{K}_{L-1},y\rangle\right)\prod_{l=1}^{L-1}\prod_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\mathcal{N}\left(h_{i}^{l}\mid 0,\tilde{K}_{l-1}\right) (7)

Where for each ll, the kernels K~l−1\tilde{K}_{l-1} themselves depend on the preactivations of layer l−1l-1, and similarly the fluctuations in α\alpha depend on the preactivations of the penultimate layer, given by

K~l>0​(x,x′)=σl+12Nl​∑i=1Nlσ⁡(hil​(x))​σ​(hil​(x′)),K0​(x,x′)=σ12d​x⋅x′\tilde{K}_{l>0}(x,x^{\prime})=\frac{\sigma_{l+1}^{2}}{N_{l}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\sigma\left(h_{i}^{l}(x)\right)\sigma\left(h_{i}^{l}(x^{\prime})\right),\quad K_{0}(x,x^{\prime})=\frac{\sigma_{1}^{2}}{d}x\cdot x^{\prime} (8)

Using statistical mechanics based notation, we define the Hamiltonian Hp,αH_{p,\alpha} and fluctuating ”partition function” ZAfZ_{A_{f}}

Hp,α​(h)\displaystyle H_{p,\alpha}\left(h\right) =α22​⟨y,K~L−1,y⟩+12​∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nl⟨hil,K~l−1−1,hil⟩,\displaystyle=\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2\left\langle y,\tilde{K}_{L-1},y\right\rangle}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\left\langle h_{i}^{l},\tilde{K}_{l-1}^{-1},h_{i}^{l}\right\rangle, (9)
log⁡ZAf​(h)\displaystyle\log Z_{A_{f}}\left(h\right) =log⁡⟨y,K~L−1,y⟩+∑l=1L−1Tr⁡log⁡K~l−1.\displaystyle=\log\left\langle y,\tilde{K}_{L-1},y\right\rangle+\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\Tr\log\tilde{K}_{l-1}.

Consequently, pAf​(α)p_{A_{f}}(\alpha) takes the form pAf​(α)=∫𝒟​h​exp⁡(−Hp,α​(h)−log⁡ZAf​(h)),p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)=\int\mathcal{D}h\,\exp\left(-H_{p,\alpha}(h)-\log Z_{A_{f}}(h)\right), where the integrand defines an effective measure on the preactivation space for a given α\alpha. We next approximate this measure per α\alpha by an analytically tractable variational estimate, qq. We follow a similar convention here: for any q,αq,\alpha, we define qα​(h):=Zq,α−1​e−Hq,α​(h)q_{\alpha}(h):=Z_{q,\alpha}^{-1}e^{-H_{q,\alpha}(h)}, requiring that the minimum value of Hq,α​(h)H_{q,\alpha}(h) be zero. For a Gaussian qq, this reduces exactly to Eq. 9, with kernels K~l−1\tilde{K}_{l-1} that are independent of hh. The variational computation follows by looking for qα​(h)q_{\alpha}(h) that minimizes the KL divergence between the measure on hh which defines pAfp_{A_{f}}, and qq. Here we provide a brief description – for the full derivation see App. C.2. By applying the Feynman–Bogoliubov inequality, we obtain an upper bound on E⁡(α)E(\alpha)

E⁡(α)≈minqα⁡(𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡(ZAf​(h)/Zq,α)]+E~q​(α)),E~q​(α)=𝔼h∼qα​[Hp,α​(h)−Hq,α​(h)]\displaystyle E(\alpha)\approx\min_{q_{\alpha}}(\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}[\log(Z_{A_{f}}(h)/Z_{q,\alpha})]+\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha)),\quad\quad\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha)=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}[H_{p,\alpha}(h)-H_{q,\alpha}(h)] (10)

We argue in App. C.4 that for α≈1\alpha\approx 1, the log terms are subleading w.r.t. E~q​(α)\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha). Defining q∗,αq_{*,\alpha} to be the measure that minimizes E~q​(α)\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha), we obtain E⁡(α)≈E~q∗​(α)E(\alpha)\approx\tilde{E}_{q_{*}}(\alpha). Next, we turn to estimating the variational energy E~q​(α)\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha) Eq. (10) for α∼1\alpha\sim 1, omitting all α\alpha indices for brevity. In App. C.1 we simplify pAfp_{A_{f}}, and show that the distribution in each layer depends only on the previous through a fluctuating non-linear operator. Next, we assume that this kernel is weakly fluctuating, and replace it with its expectation w.r.t. the variational distribution. This choice of approximation aligns with various works on deep non-linear networks, where layer-wise kernels are identified as the relevant and sufficient set of order parameters rubin_kernels_2025; fischer_critical_2024; seroussi_separation_2023; ringel_applications_2025. We further take a decoupled Gaussian variational ansatz so that q⁡(h)=∏l=1L−1∏i=1Nlql,i​(hil)q(h)=\prod_{l=1}^{L-1}\prod_{i=1}^{N_{l}}q_{l,i}(h_{i}^{l}) where ql,iq_{l,i} is Gaussian with mean μl,i\mu_{l,i} and variance Ql,iQ_{l,i}. As shown in App. C.3, the variational energy estimate is then given by

E~q∝∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nl(𝔼h∼𝒩⁡(μl,i,Ql,i)​[⟨h,Kl−1−1−Ql,i−1,h⟩]+⟨μl,i,Ql,i−1,μl,i⟩)⏟=:Δl,i+⟨y,KL−1,y⟩−1⏟=:ay,\tilde{E}_{q}\propto\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\underbrace{\left(\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{l,i},Q_{l,i})}\left[\left\langle h,K_{l-1}^{-1}-Q_{l,i}^{-1},h\right\rangle\right]+\left\langle\mu_{l,i},Q_{l,i}^{-1},\mu_{l,i}\right\rangle\right)}_{=:\Delta_{l,i}}+\underbrace{\langle y,K_{L-1},y\rangle^{-1}}_{=:a_{y}}, (11)

where we define Kl=𝔼h∼q​[K~l]K_{l}=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q}[\tilde{K}_{l}]. Here, the Δl,i\Delta_{l,i} terms arise from the difference between the approximated kernel and the actual one, and the aya_{y} term results from enforcing an alignment α≈1\alpha\approx 1. Requiring that qq minimize E~q\tilde{E}_{q} and α≈1\alpha\approx 1, we estimate E~q∝E⁡(α≈1)∝P∗\tilde{E}_{q}\propto E(\alpha\approx 1)\propto P_{*}. Another interpretation of Δl,i\Delta_{l,i}, discussed in App. In D, the excess weight is due to FL. This viewpoint is useful for FL patterns involving circuits, as the latter have a sharp imprint in weight-space. The above kernel viewpoint is, however, more general and can be used both for circuits and for more distributed learning patterns.

5 Heuristics for Manual Computation of Variational approximation

5.1 Feature Learning Patterns

While the above variational approach allows a variety of candidate qq’s, we focus on the previously mentioned set of feature-learning scenarios that have been extensively studied in the literature. Although this subset may appear restrictive, by varying behaviors among layers and between different neurons of the same layer, it already captures a wide range of phenomena. We then need to compare the variational energy (E~q\tilde{E}_{q}), as detailed in Sec. 4, for such combinations and select the minimizer. The optimal pattern is an indication of the FL that emerges in the network to enable strong alignment, as motivated in App. A.3. Concretely, per layer and neuron pre-activation (hil​(x)h^{l}_{i}(x)), we allow one of the following choices:

(1) Gaussian Process (GP). Here, ql,iq_{l,i} is a Gaussian process (GP) so that hl,i∼𝒩⁡(0,Kl−1)h_{l,i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,K_{l-1}) with Kl−1K_{l-1} defined as the expectation of the kernel defined in (8). This choice defines the ‘‘base model’’ of FL. For FCNs 55 5 For CNNs, even in the lazy regime, deeper kernels have a different input scope and hence generate a new structure., it implies that the network propagates feature structure forward without altering latent features (see Sec. 5.2). When all layers and neurons follow this distribution, the network reduces to the neural network GP (NNGP) neal_bayesian_1996, where no FL occurs. Introducing any of the patterns below in a subset of neurons enables FL to emerge.

(2) Gaussian Feature Learning (GFL). In this scenario, pre-activations remain Gaussian with zero mean, but the covariance is modified relative to the GP scenario (1): the kernel of the previous layer is amplified by a factor DD in the direction of a specific feature (e.g., an eigenfunction of Kl−1K_{l-1}) Φ∗l\Phi_{*}^{l}, one may also consider generalizations to several features). Thus, here too, the distribution is a GP but with a different covariance Ql,iQ_{l,i} given by

Ql,i​(x,x′)=Kl−1​(x,x′)+D⁡⟨Φ∗l,Kl−1,Φ∗l⟩​Φ∗l​(x)​Φ∗l​(x′).Q_{l,i}(x,x^{\prime})=K_{l-1}(x,x^{\prime})+D\langle\Phi_{*}^{l},K_{l-1},\Phi_{*}^{l}\rangle\,\Phi_{*}^{l}(x)\Phi_{*}^{l}(x^{\prime}). (12)

(3) Specialization. In this scenario, a given neuron specializes to a particular feature Φ∗l\Phi_{*}^{l} with proportionality constant μl,i\mu_{l,i}. This pattern corresponds to a Gaussian distribution which is sharply peaked around a non-zero mean μl,i​Φ∗l\mu_{l,i}\Phi_{*}^{l} 66 6 Taking equilibrated networks and increasing the amount of data, specialization was shown in rubin_grokking_2024 to emerge as a first-order phase transition where the average of preactivations suddenly shifts to μl,i\mu_{l,i}. This behavior was further associated with Grokking, suggesting a potential specialization-grokking link. . Explicitly, we define the distribution of the specialized neuron as

ql,i​(⟨hil,Φ∗l⟩)=δ⁡[⟨hil,Φ∗l⟩−μl,i],ql,i​(⟨hil,Φ⟂l⟩)=𝒩⁡(0,⟨ϕ⟂l,Kl−1,Φ⟂l⟩).q_{l,i}(\langle h_{i}^{l},\Phi_{*}^{l}\rangle)=\delta[\langle h_{i}^{l},\Phi_{*}^{l}\rangle-\mu_{l,i}],\quad q_{l,i}(\langle h_{i}^{l},\Phi_{\perp}^{l}\rangle)=\mathcal{N}(0,\langle\phi_{\perp}^{l},K_{l-1},\Phi_{\perp}^{l}\rangle). (13)

5.2 Layer-wise Feature Propagation

Since the variational energy of each layer depends on the kernel of the previous layer, an important element in our heuristic is understanding how the choice of pattern in a given layer affects the kernel and its spectrum in the subsequent layer. To this end, we define feature learning as any deviation from the baseline GP pattern (see Sec. 5.1), such as introducing a non-zero mean to the distribution (i.e., specialization) or altering its covariance structure (i.e., GFL). In our framework, a ”feature” refers either to the mean μl,i\mu_{l,i} of ql,iq_{l,i} or to an eigenfunction of its covariance operator Ql,i​(x,x′)Q_{l,i}(x,x^{\prime}).

We now outline several key claims concerning how features typically propagate between layers in FCNs. In this context, we consider a data measure that is i.i.d. Gaussian with zero mean and variance 11, not because it approximates the data well, but rather because it provides an unbiased baseline (see also lavie_demystifying_2025) for measuring function overlaps. Depending on the input, other choices can also be considered (e.g., permutation-symmetric measures over discrete tokens lavie_towards_2024). The following claims with their justifications should be understood as heuristic principles or rationalizations of empirically observed phenomena. Proving them in general or augmenting for different architectures is left for future work. For further details and empirical results, see App. C.5.

Claim (i): Neuron specialization creates a spectral spike. Assume that MM neurons in layer ll specialize on a single feature Φ∗l​(x)\Phi_{*}^{l}(x), the subsequent kernel KlK_{l} develops a new, dominant spectral feature corresponding to σ⁡(Φ∗l​(x))\sigma(\Phi^{l}_{*}(x)). The corresponding RKHS norm of this feature is amplified, scaling as 𝒪⁡(Nl/M)\mathcal{O}(N_{l}/M). Justification: When MM neurons specialize, the next layer’s kernel is approximately Kl​(x,x′)=A⁡(x,x′)+MNl​σ​(Φ∗l​(x))​σ​(Φ∗l​(x′))K_{l}(x,x^{\prime})=A(x,x^{\prime})+\tfrac{M}{N_{l}}\sigma(\Phi^{l}_{*}(x))\sigma(\Phi^{l}_{*}(x^{\prime})), where AA is the contribution from the non-specialized neurons. Treating the specialization term as a rank-1 update, the Sherman-Morrison formula shows that its RKHS norm becomes (RA−1+M/N)−1(R_{A}^{-1}+M/N)^{-1}, where RAR_{A} is the RKHS norm of AA, which satisfies RA−1≪M/NR_{A}^{-1}\ll M/N in typical high-dimensional settings.

Claim (ii): Amplified features in the pre-activation kernel create amplified higher-order features in the post-activation kernel. If a feature Φ∗l​(x)\Phi^{l}_{*}(x) in kernel KlK_{l} has its eigenvalue enhanced by a factor DD (i.e., λ∗→λ∗​D\lambda_{*}\rightarrow\lambda_{*}D), then the corresponding mm-th order power of this feature (Φ∗l)m​(x)(\Phi^{l}_{*})^{m}(x) will have the bulk of its spectral decomposition, under the downstream kernel, shifted up by DmD^{m}, with similar effect on the inverse RKHS norm. Justification: A Taylor expansion of Kl+1K_{l+1} in terms of the eigenfunctions of KlK_{l} shows that the term corresponding to (Φ∗l)m​(x)(\Phi^{l}_{*})^{m}(x) will have a coefficient scaling with (λ∗​D)m(\lambda_{*}D)^{m}. We argue that this term is difficult to span using other terms in this expansion, allowing us to treat it as a spectral spike and analyze it similarly to Claim (i). A numerical demonstration of this effect is shown in Fig. 5.

Claim (iii): Lazy layers preserve the relative scale of features from the previous layer. In the absence of FL, a properly normalized lazy layer approximately preserves the eigenspectrum of the previous kernel. If a feature Φ∗l​(x)\Phi^{l}_{*}(x) has an eigenvalue λ∗\lambda_{*} with respect to the pre-activation kernel given by Kl−1K_{l-1}, its effective eigenvalue with respect to the post-activation kernel KlK_{l} will also be proportional to λ∗\lambda_{*}. Justification: Follows from Claim (ii) taking D=1D=1.

6 Concrete Examples

We now apply the heuristic principles of Sec. 4, 5.1, 5.2 to derive sample complexity bounds in a few examples. In App. E.1, we benchmark our method on two-layer FCNs and simple CNNs with non-overlapping patches. There we reproduce both the sample complexity exponent P∗=d3/4P_{*}=d^{3/4} identified for CNNs in ringel_applications_2025 and further predict that P∗=dP_{*}=d for two-layer FCNs studying a Hermite-3 target as well as the scaling of the number of specializing neurons with width (see Fig. 2). The latter is also a setting for which the prior’s upper bound can be computed directly from E⁡(α)E(\alpha) using Large Deviation Theory, leading to a good match with experiment (Fig. 2 panel (a)).

Going to what we believe is beyond the current analytical state of the art, in App. E.3, we predict a P∗=LP_{*}=\sqrt{L}, where LL is the context length, of a softmax attention layer learning a cubic target (see Fig.  3). Another such instance, discussed in detail below, is that of a 3-layer non-linear network learning a non-linear target. In App.  A.2 we show that this approach can be extended to classification tasks as well, on non-Gaussian data. In App.  E.2 we apply our heuristics to a concrete setting, of a two-layer ReLU network trained on a parity task. We find there as well are able to predict the emergent feature pattern, which qualitatively differs from erf networks. Rather than identifying the scaling number of specializing neurons, we find that there is a finite number of neurons and we are able to predict their scale.

6.1 The Three-layer Network

Here we consider three-layer FCNs given by f⁡(x)=∑i=1N2ai​σ​(∑j=1N1wi​j(2)​σ​(wj(1)⋅x))f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{2}}a_{i}\sigma\big(\sum_{j=1}^{N_{1}}w^{(2)}_{ij}\,\sigma(w^{(1)}_{j}\cdot x)\big), where x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). We train these networks on a polynomial target of degree mm given by y⁡(x)=H​em​(w∗⋅x)y(x)=He_{m}(w_{*}\cdot x) where H​emHe_{m} is the mm-th probabilist Hermite polynomial, which is the standard polynomial choice under our choice of data measure, and w∗∈ℝSw_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} is some normalized vector. The networks are trained via Langevin dynamics welling_bayesian_nodate, with ridge parameter κ\kappa, quadratic weight decay, and standard scaling. For an extension to mean-field scaling, see App. E.1.1.

As a starting point for our analysis, consider the simplest pattern (qq“=”GP-GP), having two GP/lazy layers where taking an ll’th layer to be lazy means Ql,i=Kl−1Q_{l,i}=K_{l-1} and μl,i=0\mu_{l,i}=0. Following the choice of pattern, our goal is to estimate the scaling of E~q\tilde{E}_{q}. Examining Eq. (11), we find that the Δl=1,2,i\Delta_{l=1,2,i} contributions all cancel by our above choice of QQ’s and μ\mu’s. The only non-zero contribution thus comes from the final layer and is given by the inverse of ⟨y,K2,y⟩\langle y,K_{2},y\rangle. Because of lazy learning, K2​(x,x′)K_{2}(x,x^{\prime}) is a standard dot product FCN kernel which can be expanded as ∑n=1∞an​(x⋅x′/d)n\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_{n}(x\cdot x^{\prime}/d)^{n}, with an=O⁡(1)a_{n}=O(1) w.r.t. N1,2,d,PN_{1,2},d,P. It can then be shown that ⟨y,K2,y⟩=O⁡(d−m)\langle y,K_{2},y\rangle=O(d^{-m}). Leading to E~G​P−G​P=ay∝dm\tilde{E}_{GP-GP}=a_{y}\propto d^{m}.

Next, we consider a FL pattern wherein the first layer is GP distributed but the second has FL (qq“=”GP-Sp.). Specifically, for the l=1l=1 layer, we take Q1,i=K0;μ1,i=0Q_{1,i}=K_{0};\mu_{1,i}=0 thereby nullifying again Δ1,0\Delta_{1,0} in Eq. 11 for E~q\tilde{E}_{q}. For the second layer, we assume M2M_{2} specializing neurons (e.g., i=1..M2i=1..M_{2}) which fluctuate around the linear feature (w∗⋅xw_{*}\cdot x), while others are lazy, namely Q2,i>M2=K1,μ2,i>M2=0Q_{2,i>M_{2}}=K_{1},\mu_{2,i>M_{2}}=0 and Q2,i=1..M2=K1,μ2,i=1..M2​(x)=(w∗⋅x)Q_{2,i=1..M_{2}}=K_{1},\mu_{2,i=1..M_{2}}(x)=(w_{*}\cdot x). Examining ∑i=1N2Δ2,i\sum_{i=1}^{N_{2}}\Delta_{2,i} in Eq. 11, we get zero contributions from Δ2,i>M2=0\Delta_{2,i>M_{2}}=0 and M2​⟨(w∗⋅x),K1−1,(w∗⋅x)⟩M_{2}\langle(w_{*}\cdot x),K_{1}^{-1},(w_{*}\cdot x)\rangle from i=1..M2i=1..M_{2}. As K1K_{1} is again a simple FCN dot product kernel with no FL effects, normalized linear functions such as w∗⋅xw_{*}\cdot x have an O⁡(d)O(d) RKHS norm. We thus obtain an overall contribution to E~q\tilde{E}_{q} from the l=2l=2 layer equal to M2​dM_{2}d. Finally, we need to estimate ay=⟨y|K2|y⟩−1a_{y}=\langle y|K_{2}|y\rangle^{-1}. Note that K2K_{2} is not a standard FCN kernel anymore, since Q2Q_{2}, which contains target information, is used in its definition as the expectation of the kernel appearing in (Eq. 8). According to our feature propagation rule (i), with Φ∗=(w∗⋅x)\Phi_{*}=(w_{*}\cdot x), we have ay=N2/M2a_{y}=N_{2}/M_{2}. Given M2M_{2}, we thus obtain a variational energy of M2​d+N2/M2M_{2}d+N_{2}/M_{2}. We next need to minimize over free parameters, namely M2M_{2} leading to M2=N2/dM_{2}=\sqrt{N_{2}/d} and finally E~𝐆𝐏−𝐒𝐩.=N2​d\tilde{E}_{{\bf GP-Sp.}}=\sqrt{N_{2}d}. Provided N2N_{2} scales less than d2​m−1d^{2m-1} (N2=o⁡(d2​m−1)N_{2}=o(d^{2m-1})), this pattern is favorable to 𝐆𝐏−𝐆𝐏{\bf GP-GP}.

Finally, we consider what turns out to be the favorable pattern consisting of M1M_{1} neurons specializing on (w∗⋅x)(w_{*}\cdot x) in the first layer and all neurons in the second layer specializing H​em​(w∗⋅x)He_{m}(w_{*}\cdot x), with a small proportionality constant μ2,i=±β/N2\mu_{2,i}=\pm\sqrt{\beta/N_{2}} (qq“=”Sp.-Mag.). We refer to the second-layer pattern as magnetization. Following straightforward adaptation previous argument to this pattern, the variational energy for this pattern as well as others, for m=3m=3, can be found in Table 1.

In the non-GP qq patterns, we obtain the same scaling of E~q\tilde{E}_{q} in the proportional limit (N1∝N2∝dN_{1}\propto N_{2}\propto d), namely, P∗/κ∝dP_{*}/\kappa\propto d. This observation is validated experimentally in Fig. 3, where the transition to non-zero alignment becomes sharper in the thermodynamic limit (d→∞d\rightarrow\infty). However, the mechanism by which this scaling is realized changes. In the specialization-magnetization pattern the sample complexity scales with N11/3N_{1}^{1/3}, therefore, it increases with N1N_{1}. However, under the GP-specialization pattern, sample complexity does not scale with N1N_{1}, making this pattern preferable. This prediction is in line with experimental results (see Figs. 8 and  3 panel (c)) where increasing N1N_{1} causes the described change in FL patterns. Our prediction also accurately determines the scaling of the number of specializing neurons with N1N_{1}.

6.2 Softmax Attention

Here, we consider an attention block of the form

f⁡(X)\displaystyle f(X) =1L​∑h=1H∑a,b=1L@a​b;h​(X)​(wh⋅xb),@a​b;h​(X)=e[xa]⊤​Ah​xb​(∑c=1Le[xa]⊤​Ah​xc)−1,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{a,b=1}^{L}@_{ab;h}(X)(w_{h}\cdot x^{b}),\ \ \ @_{ab;h}(X)=e^{[x^{a}]^{\top}A_{h}x^{b}}\big(\sum_{c=1}^{L}e^{[x^{a}]^{\top}A_{h}x^{c}}\big)^{-1}, (14)

where X∈ℝL×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d}, A∈ℝd×dA\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, and xa∈ℝdx^{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the aa-th row of XX, and wh∈ℝdw_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Our prior on network weights is ∏h=1H𝒩⁡(0,Id2/d2,Ah)​𝒩​(0,Id/(d​H),wh)\prod_{h=1}^{H}\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d^{2}}/d^{2};A_{h})\,\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}/(dH);w_{h}). The only dependence on the context length LL arises from the pre-factor 1/L1/\sqrt{L}, which ensures that for Xia∼𝒩⁡(0,1)X_{i}^{a}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), we have f⁡(X)=𝒪⁡(1)f(X)=\mathcal{O}(1). The target function is given by y⁡(X)=∑a,b1L⁡(L−1)​x1a​x2b​x3by(X)=\sum_{a,b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{L(L-1)}}x^{a}_{1}x^{b}_{2}x^{b}_{3}, also normalized to be 𝒪⁡(1){\mathcal{O}}(1). Following our approach, we propose two patterns for this architecture: GP (or lazy learning) and specialization (where we take Ah∼𝒩⁡(μ​σx⊗I(d−2),Id2)A_{h}\sim{\cal N}(\mu\sigma_{x}\otimes I_{(d-2)},I_{d^{2}}) for σx=[1,0;0,1]\sigma_{x}=[1,0;0,1] and optimize over μ\mu). As detailed in  E.3, the variational energy scales as L​d3Ld^{3} for the GP pattern and as H​L​d3\sqrt{HLd^{3}} for the specialization pattern, the latter thus being favorable for HH scaling less than L​d3\sqrt{Ld^{3}}. As shown in Fig. 3, this scaling of PP with LL and dd indeed matches the dependence of the sample complexity on LL.

7 Discussion

This paper presents a novel methodology for analyzing the scaling behavior of sample complexity, through which we can also understand how distinct learning mechanisms emerge. Its strength lies in abstracting away from fine-grained details to isolate the core principles at play. We hope such a strategy would remove barriers and expedite connections between mechanistic interpretability and first-principles scientific approaches.

Limitations. Notwithstanding, several avenues for improvement remain. In particular, quantifying feature propagation in more general CNNs and transformers, and addressing multi-feature interactions as in the context of superpositionelhage2022superposition. It would also be desirable to extend our heuristic to dynamics of learning, potentially drawing insights from previous work relating equilibrium and dynamical phenomena power2022grokking; rubin_grokking_2024; bahri2021explaining; nam2024exactlysolvablemodelemergence. Since Bayesian convergence times can be slow, correctly predicting the emergence of FL in early stages of training may also be highly advantageous. Finally, in some cases, such as under mean-field scaling or vanishing ridge, overfitting effects can emerge, leaving our lower bound vacuous. Extending our approach to patterns that align only on the training set and incorporating effective ridge ideas Canatar2021 is thus desirable.

Appendix A Upper Bounds on Posterior Alignment

In this appendix, we derive bounds on the posterior probability of alignment between the network output and the target function. Our goal is to identify the scaling of the minimal sample size P∗P_{*} as a function of the input dimension, dd, required for learning. The derivation proceeds by first relating posterior probabilities of trained network outputs to the prior. While the prior probability is estimated heuristically in C, we provide here a rigorous method for computing this bound using large-deviation techniques.

A.1 The Posterior Bound

Let fΘf_{\Theta} be the output of a network with a given set of trainable weights Θ\Theta. Following standard derivations neal_bayesian_1996, the posterior distribution of possible outputs of such a network, conditioned on training on data X∈ℝP×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times d} with respect to target y:ℝd→ℝy:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (which we assume is normalized for simplicity), with MSE loss and ridge parameter κ\kappa, is given by

π⁡(f)=1Z​exp⁡(−|f⁡(X)−y⁡(X)|22​κ)​p0​(f),\pi\left(f\right)=\frac{1}{Z}\exp\left(-\frac{|f(X)-y(X)|^{2}}{2\kappa}\right)p_{0}\left(f\right), (15)

where ff and yy are applied row-wise to XX, |⋅||\cdot| is the L2L_{2} norm on the training set, p0​(f)p_{0}\left(f\right) is the prior distribution, defined by

p0​(f)=∫d​Θ​p​(Θ)​δ​[f−fΘ],p_{0}\left(f\right)=\int d\Theta\,p\left(\Theta\right)\delta\left[f-f_{\Theta}\right], (16)

We are interested in an upper bound on the posterior probability of achieving alignment ≥α\geq\alpha, where we define alignment by Af:=⟨f,y⟩=∫d​μx​f​(x)​y​(x)A_{f}:=\langle f,y\rangle=\int d\mu_{x}f(x)y(x). The prior alignment density is given by

pAf​(α)\displaystyle p_{A_{f}}(\alpha) =∫d​Θ​p​(Θ)​δ​(AfΘ−α).\displaystyle=\int d\Theta p(\Theta)\delta(A_{f_{\Theta}}-\alpha). (17)

The prior and posterior probabilities of having alignment over some threshold α\alpha are given by Prp0[Af≥α]\Pr_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right] and Prπ[Af≥α]\Pr_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right], respectively. Since the loss is positive, we have Prπ[Af≥α]≤1ZPrp0[Af≥α]\Pr_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\leq\frac{1}{Z}\Pr_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]. We proceed by obtaining a lower bound on the partition function ZZ – the normalization constant of the posterior distribution – given by

Z=𝔼Θ​[e−|fΘ​(X)−y⁡(X)|22​κ]:=∫d​Θ​p​(Θ)​e−|fΘ​(X)−y⁡(X)|22​κ.Z=\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[e^{-\frac{\left|f_{\Theta}(X)-y(X)\right|^{2}}{2\kappa}}\right]:=\int d\Theta\,p\left(\Theta\right)e^{-\frac{\left|f_{\Theta}(X)-y(X)\right|^{2}}{2\kappa}}. (18)

By Jensen’s inequality, we obtain

exp⁡(−𝔼Θ​[|fΘ​(X)−y⁡(X)|2]2​κ)<Z.\exp\left(-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\left|f_{\Theta}(X)-y(X)\right|^{2}\right]}{2\kappa}\right)<Z. (19)

Since fΘ∼𝒩⁡(0,K)f_{\Theta}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,K\right), for the NNGP kernel KK on the training data Cho, neal_bayesian_1996, it follows that 𝔼Θ​[|fΘ​(X)−y⁡(X)|2]=Tr⁡(K)+|y⁡(X)|2\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\left|f_{\Theta}(X)-y(X)\right|^{2}\right]=\mathrm{Tr}\left(K\right)+|y(X)|^{2}. Substituting this in the posterior upper bound, we obtain

Prπ[Af≥α]<exp(P​k2​κ)Prp0[Af≥α],\displaystyle\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]<\exp\left(\frac{Pk}{2\kappa}\right)\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right], (20)

log(Prπ[Af≥α])<Pk/(2κ)+log(Prp0[Af≥α]).\log\left(\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\right)<Pk/\left(2\kappa\right)+\log\left(\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\right). (21)

The r.h.s. is thermodynamically large in magnitude, crossing zero only briefly, since large negative values imply a vanishingly small probability of strong alignment, the zero crossing marks the threshold for learning. The minimal sample size necessary for learning is then

P∗=−2​κklogPrp0[Af≥α].P_{*}=-\frac{2\kappa}{k}\log\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]. (22)

We comment that P∗P_{*} provides an unlearnability bound, implying that learning cannot occur with less than P∗P_{*} . However, we find that P∗P_{*} is indeed indicative of the start of learning in the cases considered in this work. In certain settings, overfitting effects cause this bound to underestimate the true sample complexity, an effect that requires further study. In the following section, we compute the prior probability of alignment on the RHS using the Chernoff bound and large deviations theory, yielding a better estimation for P∗P_{*}.

where the subleading correction 𝒪⁡(P/do){\mathcal{O}}\left({P}/{d_{o}}\right) comes from an 𝒪⁡(1/do){\mathcal{O}}(1/d_{o}) contribution of the 2​n2n-th derivative for n≥2n\geq 2 combined with summation over dod_{o} classes and PP stems from the summation over datapoints. Thus, for a classification task, we obtain

Prπ[Af≥α]<exp(P​log⁡(do)2​κ)Prp0[Af≥α],\displaystyle\Pr\nolimits_{\pi}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]<\exp\left(\frac{P\log(d_{o})}{2\kappa}\right)\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right], (24)

Consequently, Eq. 22 applies with the necessary adjustment, replacing kk with log⁡(do)\log(d_{o}).

Our use of Wick’s Theorem to compute the disorder–averaged log-partition function over classes is closely related to the annealed and quenched free-energy calculations that appear in the statistical-physics literature on disordered systems. In that language, for fixed data 𝒟{\mathcal{D}} and random parameters Θ\Theta, the quantity −ℒ⁡(fΘ,𝒟)-{\mathcal{L}}(f_{\Theta};{\mathcal{D}}) plays the role of a random energy, and −𝔼Θ​[ℒ⁡(fΘ,𝒟)]-\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}[{\mathcal{L}}(f_{\Theta};{\mathcal{D}})] is the quenched free energy of a disordered system with dod_{o} states. Our leading term P​log⁡(do)P\log(d_{o}) is then the purely entropic contribution coming from dod_{o} equiprobable states per datapoint, in direct analogy with the N​log⁡(2)N\log(2) term in Derrida’s random–energy model Derrida1980REM for a system with 2N2^{N} configurations. In the spin-glass literature, one often replaces the quenched average 𝔼⁡[log⁡(Z)]\mathbb{E}[\log(Z)] by the annealed approximation log⁡𝔼⁡[Z]\log\mathbb{E}[Z], which follows from Jensen’s inequality for log\log and is accurate in the replica-symmetric/high-temperature phase. Our calculation stays on the quenched side and is elementary (Gaussian integrals plus Wick’s theorem), but the resulting scaling structure – an entropic log⁡(do)\log(d_{o}) term with subleading corrections controlled by the covariance of the random energies – is entirely consistent with this broader statistical-mechanics viewpoint.

A.3 The Chernoff Upper Bound

We refine the posterior bound using the Chernoff inequality. This allows us to estimate the probability of achieving alignment ≥α\geq\alpha under the prior distribution, leading to an explicit expression for the corresponding sample complexity (22). From the Chernhoff bound, we get

Prp0[Af≥α]≤inft>0e−t​α𝔼Θ[et​Af]=:e−E⁡(α).\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\leq\inf_{t>0}e^{-t\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[e^{tA_{f}}\right]=:e^{-E\left(\alpha\right)}. (25)

Substituting in (22), we obtain a new estimate

P∗=2​κk​E​(α).P_{*}=\frac{2\kappa}{k}E\left(\alpha\right). (26)

Our aim is to better estimate E⁡(α)E(\alpha). Following standard complex analysis derivation, we have

−log(Prp0[Af≥α])≥E(α)\displaystyle-\log(\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right])\geq E(\alpha) :=−log⁡(inft>0𝔼Θ​[exp⁡(t⁡(AfΘ−α))])\displaystyle:=-\log(\inf_{t>0}\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\exp\left(t\left(A_{f_{\Theta}}-\alpha\right)\right)\right])
=−log⁡(extt∈ℂ𝔼Θ​[exp⁡(i​t​(AfΘ−α))]),\displaystyle=-\log(\ext_{t\in\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\exp\left(it\left(A_{f_{\Theta}}-\alpha\right)\right)\right]), (27)

where ext\ext denotes the extremum with respect to a complex tt. Since we are in the rare event regime, we can apply a saddle point approximation to the Fourier transform of pAf​(α)p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)

pAf​(α)=12​π​∫d​t​𝔼Θ​[exp⁡(i​t​(AfΘ−α))]≈extt∈ℂ𝔼Θ​[exp⁡(i​t​(AfΘ−α))].p_{A_{f}}\!\left(\alpha\right)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int dt\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\exp\left(it\left(A_{f_{\Theta}}-\alpha\right)\right)\right]\approx\ext_{t\in\mathbb{C}}\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[\exp\left(it\left(A_{f_{\Theta}}-\alpha\right)\right)\right]. (28)

Thus, (25) can be reduced to

−logPrp0[Af≥α]≥−logpAf(α)≈E(α).-\log\Pr\nolimits_{p_{0}}\left[A_{f}\geq\alpha\right]\geq-\log p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)\approx E(\alpha). (29)

This definition of the upper bound allows for furhter simplifications.

Appendix B An Explicit Equation for the LDT Bound in Fully Connected Networks

To make our LDT analysis concrete, we now focus on FCNs. This can be trivially adapted to other architectures, however, such as CNNs and transformers. Here, we provide an explicit expression for the minimal t∗t_{*} in Eq.  25. The resulting formula involves high-dimensional, non-Gaussian integrals and is therefore highly computationally intensive. We also work out the two-layer case explicitly, where we show that the solution can be reduced to one-dimensional integrals.

We begin by specifying the architecture and notation used throughout this section. Focusing on FCNs of depth L>1L>1, we define the forward pass and parameterization explicitly:

we end up with

t∗≈9​α​π4⋅∫d​β​exp⁡(−d2​S​(β,t∗))∫d​β​(β3+2​β2)6​exp⁡(−d2​S​(β,t∗)),t_{*}\approx\frac{9\alpha\pi}{4}\cdot\frac{\int d\beta\exp\left(-\frac{d}{2}S\left(\beta;t_{*}\right)\right)}{\int d\beta\left(\frac{\beta}{\sqrt{3+2\beta^{2}}}\right)^{6}\exp\left(-\frac{d}{2}S\left(\beta;t_{*}\right)\right)}, (37)

Following the derivation for the upper bound (26), recall that we have

P∗∝−2​κ​log⁡(e−t∗​α​𝔼Θ​[et∗​Af])P_{*}\propto-2\kappa\log\left(e^{-t_{*}\alpha}\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[e^{t_{*}A_{f}}\right]\right) (38)

for k≈1k\approx 1. Following (31), we integrate out the readout weights and utilize our calculation, culminating in (37), to get

𝔼Θ​[et∗​Af]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\Theta}\left[e^{t_{*}A_{f}}\right] =𝔼W​[e12​N​∑i=1Nt∗2​Aσ,i2​(W)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{W}\left[e^{\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}t_{*}^{2}A_{\sigma,i}^{2}\left(W\right)}\right]
OPEN=∏i=1N𝔼wi∼𝒩⁡(0,1d​IdCLOSE)​[e12​N​t∗2​Aσ2​(wi)]\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{w_{i}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,\frac{1}{d}I_{d}})\left[e^{\frac{1}{2N}t_{*}^{2}A_{\sigma}^{2}(w_{i})}\right]
≈[∫d​β​exp⁡(−d2​S​(β,t∗))]N.\displaystyle\approx\left[\int d\beta\exp\left(-\frac{d}{2}S\left(\beta;t_{*}\right)\right)\right]^{N}. (39)

Finally, we arrive at the following expression for sample complexity

P∗∝2​κ​[t∗​α−N​log⁡(∫d​β​exp⁡(−d2​S​(β,t∗)))]P_{*}\propto 2\kappa\left[t_{*}\alpha-N\log\left(\int d\beta\exp\left(-\frac{d}{2}S\left(\beta;t_{*}\right)\right)\right)\right] (40)

To evaluate it, we numerically solve for t∗t_{*} in (37). The resulting t∗t_{*} is then used to numerically evaluate the one-dimensional integral in (39) over β=w⋅w∗\beta=w\cdot w_{*}. This produces the sample complexity scale in (40). These computational results are shown in Fig. 2, including predictions both for network output and weight distribution.

We can gain further insight by interpreting (39) as the partition function (i.e., the normalization factor) of a t∗t_{*}-dependent, non-Gaussian distribution. This distribution can be understood as representing the required weight configuration for achieving good alignment. While good alignment is improbable under the prior, this new distribution makes it attainable. If this distribution represents the optimal path to alignment within the prior, it is reasonable to infer that it will correspond to the FL patterns in the posterior. Indeed, as illustrated in Fig. 2, this is precisely the case, as the posterior weight distribution is closely approximated by the prior alignment distribution we predict. It is this observation that motivates the reasoning in the following sections, by guessing various FL patterns that result in good alignment in the prior, we can deduce the actual distribution in the posterior. We can compare different guesses and determine which of the patterns is most likely to emerge.

C.2 Variational approximation

Turning back to the alignment density pAfp_{A_{f}}, we can substitute the result from the previous section so that

pAf(α)=∫𝒟hexp(−(Hp~​(h)+α22​κA​(hL−1))⏟=:−Hp,α​(h)−(12​log⁡κA​(hL−1)+log⁡Zp~​(h))⏟=:log⁡ZAf​(h))p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)=\int\mathcal{D}h\exp\left(-\underbrace{\left(H_{\tilde{p}}\left(h\right)+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2\kappa_{A}\left(h^{L-1}\right)}\right)}_{=:-H_{p,\alpha}\left(h\right)}-\underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2}\log\kappa_{A}(h^{L-1})+\log Z_{\tilde{p}}(h)\right)}_{=:\log Z_{A_{f}}(h)}\right) (49)

We are interested in computing E⁡(α)E(\alpha), which is given by

E(α)=−logpAf(α)=−log∫𝒟hexp(−Hp,α(h))/ZAf(h).E(\alpha)=-\log p_{A_{f}}(\alpha)=-\log\int\mathcal{D}h\exp\left(-H_{p,\alpha}\left(h\right)\right)/Z_{A_{f}}(h). (50)

Since the integral over hh is generally intractable, we turn to a variational approximation. The goal of this estimate is to find a simpler, tractable distribution qα​(h)q_{\alpha}(h) that is in some sense ”close” to the true pre-activation density exp⁡(−Hp,α​(h))\exp(-H_{p,\alpha}(h)) per alpha. We thus define our variational distribution in a similar Hamiltonian

qα​(h)=1Zq,α​exp⁡(−Hq,α​(h)),q_{\alpha}(h)=\frac{1}{Z_{q,\alpha}}\exp(-H_{q,\alpha}(h)), (51)

where Hq,αH_{q,\alpha} satisfies minh⁡Hq,α​(h)=0\min_{h}H_{q,\alpha}(h)=0, and Zq,αZ_{q,\alpha} is the partition function given by Zq,α=∫𝒟​h​exp⁡(−Hq,α​(h))Z_{q,\alpha}=\int\mathcal{D}h\exp\left(-H_{q,\alpha}\left(h\right)\right). This choice results in a unique definition of Hq,α,Zq,αH_{q,\alpha},\ Z_{q,\alpha} for each distribution qαq_{\alpha}. The Feynman-Bogoliubov inequality provides a rigorous definition of closeness between exp⁡(−Hp,α​(h))\exp(-H_{p,\alpha}(h)) and qα​(h)q_{\alpha}(h). This inequality establishes an upper bound on E⁡(α)E(\alpha) which depends on the choice of qq. The Feynman-Bogoliubov inequality bogolubov_introduction_2009 states that for any qq

−log⁡(∫𝒟​h​e−Hp,α​(h)/ZAf​(h))≤−log⁡Zq,α+𝔼h∼qα​[Hp,α​(h)−Hq,α​(h)+log⁡ZAf​(h)]-\log\left(\int\mathcal{D}he^{-H_{p,\alpha}\left(h\right)}/Z_{A_{f}}(h)\right)\leq-\log Z_{q,\alpha}+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[H_{p,\alpha}(h)-H_{q,\alpha}(h)+\log Z_{A_{f}}(h)\right] (52)

where 𝔼h∼qα​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}[\cdot] is the expectation over hh with respect to the distribution qαq_{\alpha}. Recalling that E⁡(α)=−log⁡pAf​(α)E(\alpha)=-\log p_{A_{f}}(\alpha), this inequality can be used to simplify the bound

E⁡(α)≤𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡(ZAf​(h)/Zq,α)]+𝔼h∼qα​[Hp,α​(h)−Hq,α​(h)]=:E~q​(α),E(\alpha)\leq\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log(Z_{A_{f}}(h)/Z_{q,\alpha})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[H_{p,\alpha}(h)-H_{q,\alpha}(h)\right]=:\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha), (53)

We can estimate E⁡(α)E(\alpha) by taking qαq_{\alpha} which minimizes the upper bound (53). In the following sections we turn to compute the upper bound. Since we consider only α≈1\alpha\approx 1, we drop α\alpha in what follows.

When NL−1N_{L-1} is large, κA\kappa_{A} is weakly fluctuating with hL−1h^{L-1}, since it is a sum of NL−1N_{L-1} random variables. Denoting κ¯Af=𝔼h∼p~​(h)​[κA​(hL−1)]\overline{\kappa}_{A_{f}}=\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\tilde{p}\left(h\right)}\left[\kappa_{A}\left(h^{L-1}\right)\right], we have

𝔼h∼q1​[Hp,1​(h)−Hq,1​(h)]≈12​κ¯A+𝔼h∼q​[Hp~​(h)−Hq​(h)]\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{1}}\left[H_{p,1}(h)-H_{q,1}(h)\right]\approx\frac{1}{2\overline{\kappa}_{A}}+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q}\left[H_{\tilde{p}}(h)-H_{q}(h)\right] (54)

to leading order (where q≡q1q\equiv q_{1}), so that

E~q​(1)≈12​κ¯A+𝔼h∼q​[Hp~​(h)−Hq​(h)]+𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡(ZAf​(h)/Zq,α)].\tilde{E}_{q}\left(1\right)\approx\frac{1}{2\overline{\kappa}_{A}}+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q}\left[H_{\tilde{p}}\left(h\right)-H_{q}\left(h\right)\right]+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log(Z_{A_{f}}(h)/Z_{q,\alpha})\right]. (55)

We show in C.4 that the expectation of log term- 𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡(ZAf​(h)/Zq,α)]\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log(Z_{A_{f}}(h)/Z_{q,\alpha})\right] is subleading and thus can be neglected. In essence, our variational ansatzes constrain deviations from the GP to a sub-extensive subset of feature directions, such that the resulting corrections do not scale extensively with system size or parameter count. Moreover, since these corrections enter logarithmically, their contribution becomes further subleading. Thus, we have

E~q≈12​κ¯A+𝔼h∼q​[Hp~​(h)−Hq​(h)]\tilde{E}_{q}\approx\frac{1}{2\overline{\kappa}_{A}}+\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q}\left[H_{\tilde{p}}\left(h\right)-H_{q}\left(h\right)\right] (56)

The problem has now been reduced to minimizing E~q\tilde{E}_{q} with respect to a choice of variational distribution q⁡(h)q(h). If we find the optimal q∗q_{*} that minimizes E~q\tilde{E}_{q}, we obtain our best estimate for the energy, when α≈1\alpha\approx 1,

E⁡(α≈1)≈E~q∗.E(\alpha\approx 1)\approx\tilde{E}_{q_{*}}. (57)

C.3 Approximate Variational Energy

Our final task is to compute the variational energy E~q​(α)\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha) given our variational density qq. Although we work with Gaussian qq’s that are layer-wise and neuron-wise decoupled, this computation is nevertheless challenging due to the presence of hlh^{l}, dependence on [K~l]−1[\tilde{K}_{l}]^{-1}, and the trace term Tr⁡log⁡(K~l)\Tr\log(\tilde{K}_{l}). In the spirit of kernel adaptation ringel_applications_2025, we assume the fluctuations of K~l\tilde{K}_{l} are sufficiently small and only keep the leading order dependence which dominates E~q​(α)\tilde{E}_{q}(\alpha). In this context, this means replacing the fluctuating kernel K~l\tilde{K}_{l} with its expectation with respect to qq and KlK_{l} given by

Kl(x,x′)=σl+12Nl∑i=1Nl𝔼hil∼q(hl)][σ(hil(x))σ(hil(x′))].K_{l}\left(x,x^{\prime}\right)=\frac{\sigma_{l+1}^{2}}{N_{l}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\mathbb{E}_{h_{i}^{l}\sim q(h^{l})]}[\sigma(h_{i}^{l}\left(x\right))\sigma(h_{i}^{l}\left(x^{\prime}\right))]. (58)

Following this substitution, we obtain

Hp~​(h)=12​∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nl⟨hil,[Kl−1]−1​hil⟩H_{\tilde{p}}(h)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\langle h_{i}^{l},[K_{l-1}]^{-1}h_{i}^{l}\rangle (59)

and obtain our final tractable expression for the variational energy

E~q∝12​⟨y,KL−1,y⟩−1+12​𝔼h∼q​[∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nl⟨hil,Kl−1−1,hil⟩−Hq​(h)].\tilde{E}_{q}\propto\frac{1}{2}\left\langle y,K_{L-1},y\right\rangle^{-1}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q}\left[\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\left\langle h_{i}^{l},K_{l-1}^{-1},h_{i}^{l}\right\rangle-H_{q}\left(h\right)\right]. (60)

Since p~\tilde{p} is fully decoupled layer and neuron-wise, we similarly take a decoupled variational ansatz so that q⁡(h)=∏l=1L−1∏i=1Nlql,i​(hil)q(h)=\prod_{l=1}^{L-1}\prod_{i=1}^{N_{l}}q_{l,i}(h_{i}^{l}). Further taking ql,iq_{l,i} to be Gaussian with mean μl,i\mu_{l,i} and variance Ql,iQ_{l,i}, we obtain

E~q=12​⟨y,KL−1,y⟩−1+12​∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nl{𝔼hil∼ql,i​[⟨hil,[Kl−1]−1−Ql,i−1,hil⟩]+⟨μl,i,Ql,i−1,μl,i⟩}\tilde{E}_{q}=\frac{1}{2}\left\langle y,K_{L-1},y\right\rangle^{-1}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}{\left\{\mathbb{E}_{h_{i}^{l}\sim q_{l,i}}\left[\left\langle h_{i}^{l},\left[K_{l-1}\right]^{-1}-Q_{l,i}^{-1},h_{i}^{l}\right\rangle\right]+\left\langle\mu_{l,i},Q_{l,i}^{-1},\mu_{l,i}\right\rangle\right\}} (61)

Minimizing the above over all Gaussian qq’s results in complex non-linear equations, which we wish to avoid. Instead, we propose minimizing over a small subset of qq’s, which we refer to as FL patterns. We look to minimize E~q\tilde{E}_{q} over this finite set and take that to be our variational energy. A summary of all patterns can be found in Fig.  4.

C.3.1 Comparison to Adaptive Kernel Approximation

The similarities and differences between the approach developed here and the adaptive methods discussed in Seroussi2023, ringel_applications_2025 are worth examining. In those works, p~\tilde{p} is similarly approximated using a mean-field expansion, with two key differences: The chosen mean and the order of expansion around the mean. The fluctuating kernel in these works K~l−1\tilde{K}_{l-1} is expanded around its self-consistent mean Kl−1|p~K_{l-1\mid\tilde{p}}, rather than the variational expectation introduced here. The self-consistent mean kernel is defined as

Kl>0|p~​(x,x′)\displaystyle K_{l>0\mid\tilde{p}}(x,x^{\prime}) =σl+12Nl​∑i=1Nl𝔼hil∼p~​(h)​[σ⁡(hil​(x))​σ​(hil​(x′))],\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{l+1}^{2}}{N_{l}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\mathbb{E}_{h_{i}^{l}\sim\tilde{p}(h)}\!\left[\sigma(h_{i}^{l}(x))\,\sigma(h_{i}^{l}(x^{\prime}))\right], (62)
K0|p~​(x,x′)\displaystyle K_{0\mid\tilde{p}}(x,x^{\prime}) =σ02d​x⋅x′.\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{0}^{2}}{d}\,x\cdot x^{\prime}.

We define the kernel fluctuations relative to this mean by Δ​Kl−1\Delta K_{l-1}, such that K~l−1=Kl−1|p~+Δ​Kl−1\tilde{K}_{l-1}=K_{l-1\mid\tilde{p}}+\Delta K_{l-1}. The adaptive approximations assume that these fluctuations are weak, i.e., Δ​Kl−1≪Kl−1|p~\Delta K_{l-1}\ll K_{l-1\mid\tilde{p}}, and retain all terms up to order 𝒪⁡(Δ​Kl−1)\mathcal{O}(\Delta K_{l-1}), whereas in this work we consider only the zeroth-order term in Δ​Kl−1\Delta K_{l-1}. Taking such an approximation in the self-consistent setting would yield the GP distribution, since no feature-learning corrections would be taken into account. In our proposed methodology, because the variational expectation already incorporates feature-learning effects, the simpler expansion can instead be employed.

C.4 Justification for Neglecting the Partition Function Ratio

Here we argue that the logarithmic ratio of partition functions, 𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡(ZAf​(h)/Zq)]\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log(Z_{A_{f}}(h)/Z_{q})\right], is sub-leading relative to the variational energy term E~q\tilde{E}_{q} (defined in Sec. C.2). We show that this holds for all feature learning patterns considered in this work (Sec. 5.1): GP, GFL, and specialization. Substituting the definition of ZAf​(h)Z_{A_{f}}(h) we obtain:

𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡ZAf​(h)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log Z_{A_{f}}(h)\right] =𝔼qα​[12​log⁡κA​(hL−1)]+12​∑l=1L−1Tr⁡𝔼qα​[log⁡(K~l−1)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{q_{\alpha}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\log\kappa_{A}(h^{L-1})\right]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\Tr\mathbb{E}_{q_{\alpha}}\left[\log(\tilde{K}_{l-1})\right] (63)

We assume that for sufficiently wide networks the fluctuations are weak, so that at least in terms of scales we can approximate

...≈log𝔼qα[12κA(hL−1)]+12∑l=1L−1Trlog𝔼qα[(K~l−1)]...\approx\log\mathbb{E}_{q_{\alpha}}\left[\frac{1}{2}\kappa_{A}(h^{L-1})\right]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\Tr\log\mathbb{E}_{q_{\alpha}}\left[(\tilde{K}_{l-1})\right]

So that we obtain

𝔼h∼qα​[log⁡ZAf​(h)]≈12​∑l=1L−1Tr⁡log⁡Kl−1+12​log​κ¯A\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{\alpha}}\left[\log Z_{A_{f}}(h)\right]\approx\frac{1}{2}\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\Tr\log K_{l-1}+\frac{1}{2}\log{\overline{\kappa}_{A}} (64)

Recalling that E~q\tilde{E}_{q} scales linearly with κ¯A−1\overline{\kappa}_{A}^{-1}, we can indeed justify neglecting the term log⁡κ¯A\log{\overline{\kappa}_{A}} as it is subleading for small κ¯A\overline{\kappa}_{A}. We will show that the remaining terms can be neglected as well. Using the eigendecomposition of the kernel (58), Kl−1​(x,x′)=∑klλkl​Φkl​(x)​Φkl​(x′)K_{l-1}(x,x^{\prime})=\sum_{k_{l}}\lambda_{k_{l}}\Phi_{k_{l}}(x)\Phi_{k_{l}}(x^{\prime}), the Gaussian integral for a single neuron in layer ll evaluates to ∏kl2​π​λkl\prod_{k_{l}}\sqrt{2\pi\lambda_{k_{l}}}. The logarithm of the full partition function is then

log⁡Zp=∑l=1L−1Nl​log⁡(∏kl2​π​λkl)=:∑l=1L−1Nl​log⁡Zpl,\log Z_{p}=\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}N_{l}\log\left(\prod_{k_{l}}\sqrt{2\pi\lambda_{k_{l}}}\right)=:\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}N_{l}\log Z_{p}^{l}, (65)

where we have defined log⁡Zpl\log Z_{p}^{l} as the single-neuron log-partition function under the GP prior. As described in the main text, we consider variational distributions qq that fully factorize over layers and neurons. Thus, we can write

logZq=∑l=1L−1∑i=1Nllog∫Dhilql,i(hil)=:∑l=1L−1∑i=1NllogZql,i.\log Z_{q}=\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\log\int Dh_{i}^{l}\,q_{l,i}(h_{i}^{l})=:\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\log Z_{q}^{l,i}. (66)

Combining these results, the log-ratio of the partition functions decomposes into a sum over per-neuron contributions. We aim to show that, for each neuron, this term is sub-dominant compared to the corresponding term in the variational energy E~q\tilde{E}_{q}. Recall (61) that

E~q=12​⟨y,KL−1,y⟩+∑l=1L−1∑i=1NlΔl,i,\tilde{E}_{q}=\frac{1}{2}\langle y,K_{L}^{-1},y\rangle+\sum_{l=1}^{L-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l}}\Delta_{l,i}, (67)

where the per-neuron cost Δl,i\Delta_{l,i} is

Δl,i:=12​𝔼h∼ql,i​[⟨h,Kl−1−1−Ql,i−1,h⟩+⟨μl,i,Ql,i−1,μl,i⟩].\Delta_{l,i}:=\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{E}_{h\sim q_{l,i}}\left[\langle h,K_{l-1}^{-1}-Q_{l,i}^{-1},h\rangle+\langle\mu_{l,i},Q_{l,i}^{-1},\mu_{l,i}\rangle\right]. (68)

Our goal is to show that, for each feature learning pattern, Δl,i+(log⁡Zql,i−log⁡Zpl)\Delta_{l,i}+(\log Z_{q}^{l,i}-\log Z_{p}^{l}) scales like Δl,i\Delta_{l,i}.

C.5 Kernel Feature Propagation

Since the cost of each layer depends on the kernel of the previous layer, an important element of our heuristic is understanding how the choice of pattern in the previous layer affects the kernel and its spectrum. Recall that we denote the pre-activation of the current layer by hl​(x)h^{l}(x), and of the previous layer by hl−1​(x){h}^{l-1}(x), where hl−1​(x){h}^{l-1}(x) is the width Nl−1N_{l-1} pre-activation vector of the previous layer. Let hil−1h^{l-1}_{i} be distributed according to some candidate Gaussian distribution qi′​(hl−1)q^{\prime}_{i}(h^{l-1}). We wish to understand how this choice of qi′​(hl−1)q^{\prime}_{i}(h^{l-1}) affects the kernel of the next layer given by

Kl−1​(x,x′)\displaystyle K_{l-1}(x,x^{\prime}) =Nl−1−1​∑i=1Nl−1𝔼hil−1​(x)∼qi​[σ⁡(hil−1​(x))​σ​(hil−1​(x′))]=:∑i=1Nl−1Kl−1,i​(x,x′),\displaystyle=N_{l-1}^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l-1}}\mathbb{E}_{h^{l-1}_{i}(x)\sim q_{i}}[\sigma(h^{l-1}_{i}(x))\sigma(h^{l-1}_{i}(x^{\prime}))]=:\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l-1}}{K_{l-1,i}(x,x^{\prime})}, (70)

where we took σl2=1\sigma_{l}^{2}=1 for brevity.

Claim (i): Neuron specialization creates a spectral spike. Assume we have an operator of the form K⁡(x,x′)=A⁡(x,x′)+c​σ​(Φ⁡(x))​σ​(Φ⁡(x′))K(x,x^{\prime})=A(x,x^{\prime})+c\sigma(\Phi(x))\sigma(\Phi(x^{\prime})) for some constant cc. We wish to understand the behavior of the RKHS norm of σ⁡(Φ)\sigma(\Phi) with respect to the above operator. Using the Sherman-Morrison formula, we obtain

[A+c​σ​(Φ)​σ​(Φ)⊤]−1\displaystyle[A+c\sigma(\Phi)\sigma(\Phi)^{\top}]^{-1} =A−1−A−1​c​σ​(Φ)​σ​(Φ)⊤​A−11+c​σ​(Φ)⊤​A−1​σ​(Φ),\displaystyle=A^{-1}-\frac{A^{-1}c\sigma(\Phi)\sigma(\Phi)^{\top}A^{-1}}{1+c\sigma(\Phi)^{\top}A^{-1}\sigma(\Phi)}, (71)

where v​v⊤vv^{\top} denotes the outer product. Consequently, the RKHS norm of σ⁡(Φ)\sigma(\Phi) with respect to KK is given by

RK≡σ​(Φ)⊤​[A+c​σ​(Φ)​σ​(Φ)⊤]−1​σ​(Φ)=RA−RA2​c1+RA​c=RA1+RA​c<1/c\displaystyle R_{K}\equiv\sigma(\Phi)^{\top}[A+c\sigma(\Phi)\sigma(\Phi)^{\top}]^{-1}\sigma(\Phi)=R_{A}-\frac{R_{A}^{2}c}{1+R_{A}c}=\frac{R_{A}}{1+R_{A}c}<1/c (72)

where RAR_{A} is its RKHS norm w.r.t. A−1A^{-1}. Typically, we would consider large values of RAR_{A}. Thus, if we have c​RA≫1cR_{A}\gg 1, then- RA1+RA​c≈c−1\frac{R_{A}}{1+R_{A}c}\approx c^{-1}, thereby justifying Claim (i).

Corollary 1.

If MM of NlN_{l} neurons are specialized in a given layer with the rest remaining Gaussian with zero mean, then we can substitute c=Nl/Mc=N_{l}/M in the above, and obtain RKl=Nl/MR_{K_{l}}=N_{l}/M.

Corollary 2.

If all neurons are specialized with proportionality constant β\sqrt{\beta}, then we can substitute c=βc=\beta in the above, and take A=ϵ​IA=\epsilon I as a regularizer, with ϵ→0\epsilon\rightarrow 0, so that RA→∞R_{A}\rightarrow\infty, and we obtain RKl=βR_{K_{l}}=\beta.

Claim (ii): Amplified features in the pre-activation kernel create amplified higher-order features in the post-activation kernel. We begin by considering the Gaussian case, where hil​(x)∼𝒩⁡(0,Ql)h^{l}_{i}(x)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{l}) for all ii. Since KlK_{l} is a dot product kernel for an FCN, we can expand the expectation in (58) to obtain

Kl​(x,x′)\displaystyle K_{l}(x,x^{\prime}) =∑a=1∞(Ql​(x,x′))a​Fa​(x,x′),\displaystyle=\sum_{a=1}^{\infty}(Q_{l}(x,x^{\prime}))^{a}\ F_{a}(x,x^{\prime}), (73)

where Ql​(x,x′)Q_{l}(x,x^{\prime}) is a function of x⋅x′x\cdot x^{\prime} and Fa​(x,x′)F_{a}(x,x^{\prime}) is a function of |x|2|x|^{2} and |x′|2|x^{\prime}|^{2} derived by expanding the resulting Cho and Saul kernel associated with the activation function σ\sigma [Cho, §2.3]. We further assume that Ql​(x,x)∼𝒪⁡(1)+Q_{l}(x,x)\sim\mathcal{O}(1)+small fluctuations. This is a reasonable assumption to make for Gaussian data in high dimensions where |x|2=d±d|x|^{2}=d\pm\sqrt{d}. For more general datasets, one should either verify this or apply layer-normalization (as done below for the case of data with power-law covariance spectrum).

Using its Mercer decomposition Ql​(x,x′)=∑kλk​Φk​(x)​Φk​(x′)Q_{l}(x,x^{\prime})=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\Phi_{k}(x)\Phi_{k}(x^{\prime}) , we have

Kl​(x,x′)\displaystyle K_{l}(x,x^{\prime}) ∝∑kλk​Φk​(x)​Φk​(x′)+∑k1,k2λk1​λk2​Φk1​(x)​Φk2​(x)​Φk1​(x′)​Φk2​(x′)+…\displaystyle\propto\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\Phi_{k}(x)\Phi_{k}(x^{\prime})+\sum_{k_{1},k_{2}}\lambda_{k_{1}}\lambda_{k_{2}}\Phi_{k_{1}}(x)\Phi_{k_{2}}(x)\Phi_{k_{1}}(x^{\prime})\Phi_{k_{2}}(x^{\prime})+... (74)

Next, we ask how enhancing a certain λk\lambda_{k} by a factor DD affects the post-activation kernel Kl​(x,x′)K_{l}(x,x^{\prime}). Let λk∗\lambda_{k_{*}} be some eigenvalue of QlQ_{l} corresponding to the eigenfunction Φ∗​(x)\Phi_{*}(x). It can be potentially adapted via GFL (λk∗→D​λ∗\lambda_{k_{*}}\rightarrow D\lambda_{*} where D​λ∗<1D\lambda_{*}<1). Then the Kl,iK_{l,i} RKHS norm of any feature of the form ∑n=1man​Φλ∗n​(x)\sum_{n=1}^{m}a_{n}\Phi^{n}_{\lambda_{*}}(x) scales like 𝒪⁡((λ∗​D)−m)\mathcal{O}((\lambda_{*}D)^{-m}) (assuming am=𝒪⁡(1)a_{m}=\mathcal{O}(1)). Indeed, consider the case m=2m=2 and examine

Kl​(x,x′)∝∑kDk​λk​Φk​(x)​Φk​(x′)+∑k1,k2Dk1​Dk2​λk1​λk2​Φk1​(x)​Φk2​(x)​Φk1​(x′)​Φk2​(x′)+…\displaystyle K_{l}(x,x^{\prime})\propto\sum_{k}D_{k}\lambda_{k}\Phi_{k}(x)\Phi_{k}(x^{\prime})+\sum_{k_{1},k_{2}}D_{k_{1}}D_{k_{2}}\lambda_{k_{1}}\lambda_{k_{2}}\Phi_{k_{1}}(x)\Phi_{k_{2}}(x)\Phi_{k_{1}}(x^{\prime})\Phi_{k_{2}}(x^{\prime})+... (75)

with Dk=DD_{k}=D when λk=λ∗\lambda_{k}=\lambda_{*} and Dk=1D_{k}=1 otherwise. The argument proceeds by treating the term Φ∗m​(x)​Φ∗m​(x′)\Phi^{m}_{*}(x)\Phi^{m}_{*}(x^{\prime}) as a rank-1 spike. Substituting KlK_{l} for KK, (D​λ∗)m(D\lambda_{*})^{m} for cc, and Φm\Phi^{m} for σ⁡(Φ)\sigma(\Phi) in Claim (i), we obtain RKl=(RA−1+(D​λ∗)m)−1R_{K_{l}}=(R_{A}^{-1}+(D\lambda_{*})^{m})^{-1}.

The important observation/assumption here is that, for sufficiently large DD, RA​(D​λ∗)m≫1R_{A}(D\lambda_{*})^{m}\gg 1 so that RKl≈(D​λ∗)−mR_{K_{l}}\approx(D\lambda_{*})^{-m}. This is supported numerically in Figs. 5 and 6. Our analytical reasoning is that the subspace effectively described by the kernel KlK_{l} is a negligible portion of the total function space. This is either because the rank of KlK_{l} is constrained by network width NlN_{l} or its spectrum λk\lambda_{k} exhibits rapid decay. Our analytical rationalization for this is as follows. Either because in a real network, the rank of the kernel KlK_{l} is bounded by the network width NlN_{l} or because the spectrum λk\lambda_{k} falls down quickly, the effective span of the first term and subsequent terms covers only a negligible fraction of the total function space. In this large function space, it is unlikely that a feature like Φ∗m\Phi^{m}_{*} is fully contained within this span. If this is the case, its RKHS norm with respect to the base kernel would be large, motivating our observation/assumption.

In Fig. 5, we consider two ReLU-activated layers of an FCN (L=4L=4) and Gaussian i.i.d. data x∈ℝd,x∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},x\sim{{\mathcal{N}}}(0,I_{d}). We obtain the empirical NNGP kernel after the first ReLU layer of width N1=2000N_{1}=2000. Diagonalizing the kernel (Kl=2K_{l=2}) on P=6000P=6000 sample points {xν}ν=1P\{x_{\nu}\}_{\nu=1}^{P}, we choose Φ∗​(x)\Phi_{*}(x) to be the d/2d/2 highest eigenvalue. We then look for the best weight vector a∈ℝN1a\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{1}} satisfying Φ∗​(xν)≈∑i=1N1ai​ReLU​(Wi⋅xν)\Phi_{*}(x_{\nu})\approx\sum_{i=1}^{N_{1}}a_{i}\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{i}\cdot x_{\nu}), where WiW_{i} are the input layer weights used to generate Kl=2K_{l=2}. We draw the rows of W∈ℝN2×N1W\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{2}\times N_{1}} i.i.d. with Wi∼𝒩⁡(0,I/N1+(D−1)​a^​a^⊤/N1)W_{i}\sim{\mathcal{N}}\left(0,I/N_{1}+(D-1)\hat{a}\hat{a}^{\top}/N_{1}\right), where a^=a/a⊤​a\hat{a}=a/\sqrt{a^{\top}a}. This mimics the GFL effect. Finally, we compute the kernel empirical kernel following another ReLU layer and compute the RKHS norm of Φ∗2​(x)\Phi_{*}^{2}(x) with mean removed, omitting eigenvalues which are zero up to machine precision (for P>N2P>N_{2}, P−N2P-N_{2} such eigenvalues are to be expected).

To prevent strong fluctuations of K2​(x,x)K_{2}(x,x) (i.e., Q2​(x,x)Q_{2}(x,x) of Claim (ii)), which are now not suppressed at d→∞d\rightarrow\infty we apply layer normalization between the two activated ReLU layers.
