Appendix D E~\tilde{E} and Δℓ\Delta_{\ell} in Weight Space

In the main text, we focused on a function space formulation for E~\tilde{E}, using pre-activations, GP distributions (qq) for hlh^{l}, and kernel operators. This formulation facilitated the combination of GP-like learning mechanisms and circuit/specialization-based mechanisms. In some cases however, it is more natural to work in weight space (see also Guth2024 for a weight-space picture analogous to kernel adaptation). One such example is CNNs, for which the distribution of the input layer convolutional-patch-dependent pre-activations, is more readily described in terms of shared input weights. Another example would be an i0i_{0}-th neuron specializing on some j0j_{0} neuron of the upstream layer, which implies a delta-function distribution around Wi0​j∼δj,j​0W_{i_{0}j}\sim\delta_{j,j0}. Accordingly, we wish to express Δl,i\Delta_{l,i} of (68) in weight space. For simplicity, we focus on distributions with zero mean.

To this end, we consider some pre-activation in layer ll and write it in terms of layer weights namely, hi0l​(x)=∑i=1Nl−1Wi0​il​σ​(hil−1​(x))h^{l}_{i_{0}}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{l-1}}W^{l}_{i_{0}i}\sigma(h^{l-1}_{i}(x)). For compactness, we henceforth take Wi0​il→ai,hi0l→hlW^{l}_{i_{0}i}\rightarrow a_{i},h^{l}_{i_{0}}\rightarrow h^{l}. We next treat the hil−1h^{l-1}_{i}’s as independent draws from ql−1,i=ql−1q_{l-1,i}=q_{l-1}, consistent with the kernel adaptation approximation, which removes correlations between pre-activation. To avoid operator algebra and work solely with matrices, we consider extremely many (P′P^{\prime}) draws {xν}ν=1P′\{x_{\nu}\}_{\nu=1}^{P^{\prime}} from d​μxd\mu_{x} and define the (l−1l-1)-th feature matrix with entries

Fi​νl−1:=σ(hil−1(xν)),i=1,…,Nl−1,ν=1,…,P′\displaystyle F_{i\nu}^{l-1}:=\sigma(h^{l-1}_{i}(x_{\nu})),\quad i=1,\ldots,N_{l-1},\quad\nu=1,\ldots,P^{\prime}

Note that for large Nl−1N_{l-1}, [(Fl−1)⊤​Fl−1]μ​ν/Nl−1\left[\left(F^{l-1}\right)^{\top}F^{l-1}\right]_{\mu\nu}/N_{l-1}, via the law of large numbers, concentrates to its averages under qq and thus approaches Kl−1​(xμ,xν)K_{l-1}(x_{\mu},x_{\nu}).

We next revisit the inter-layer action for l,l−1l,l-1 appearing Eq. (48 given by ⟨h,K~−1,h⟩\langle h,\tilde{K}^{-1},h\rangle and note that (i) K~\tilde{K} upon freezing hl−1h^{l-1} at some typical value as done above, K~=F⊤​F/Nl−1\tilde{K}=F^{\top}F/N_{l-1} (ii) the inverse operation is to be understood as a pseudo inverse ((..)+(..)^{+}) which removes the contribution of the null space of this (generically) rank-Nl−1N_{l-1} operator. Following this and the linear relation between hlh^{l} and aa, we have that

⟨h,K~l−1+,h⟩\displaystyle\langle h,\tilde{K}_{l-1}^{+},h\rangle =aT​F​[F⊤​F/Nl−1]+​F⊤​a=Nl−1​a⊤​a.\displaystyle=a^{T}F[F^{\top}F/N_{l-1}]^{+}F^{\top}a=N_{l-1}a^{\top}a. (76)

We thus obtain a reasonable result: The RKHS term, which regulates the pre-activations, is equal to the weight-decay term associated with the aa’s that generated that hh.

Following this rewriting, one can now repeat our variational approximation in weight space.This results in an analogous formula to Eq. 11 with qlq_{l} denoting a Gaussian distribution on aa’s (a∼𝒩⁡[a¯l,Σl]a\sim{\cal N}[\bar{a}^{l},\Sigma_{l}]), and Kl−1K_{l-1} (the covariance of the hh’s in the action) replaced by I/Nl−1I/N_{l-1} (the covariance of aa’s in the action).

All in all we obtain the following weight space version of the contribution of the ii’th neuron to E~q\tilde{E}_{q}, namely

Δl,i\displaystyle\Delta_{l,i} =𝔼a∼𝒩⁡(a¯,Σl)​[a⊤​[Nl−1​I−Σl−1]​a]+a¯T​Σl−1​a¯\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{a},\Sigma_{l})}\left[a^{\top}[N_{l-1}I-\Sigma_{l}^{-1}]a\right]+\bar{a}^{T}\Sigma_{l}^{-1}\bar{a} (77)

Appendix E Application of Heuristics for Additional Architectures

E.1 Regression tasks in Two-layer Networks

In the two-layer setting, an exact solution can be obtained, so we begin by comparing our heuristic approach to the exact solution. In this case, we consider both two-layer FCNs as well as CNNs with non-overlapping convolution windows. Together, these are given by

f⁡(x)=∑i=1Nw∑j=1Nwi​j(2)​σ​(wj(1)⋅xi),f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}w^{(2)}_{ij}\,\sigma(w^{(1)}_{j}\cdot x_{i}), (78)

where x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). We take d=Nw​Sd=N_{w}S so that wj,xi∈ℝSw_{j},x_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{S}. The vector xix_{i} is given by the ((i−1)​S+1)((i-1)S+1)-th to i​SiS-th coordinates of xx. We train these networks on a polynomial target of degree mm given by y⁡(x)=∑i=1NwH​em​(w∗⋅xi)y(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}He_{m}(w_{*}\cdot x_{i}) where H​emHe_{m} is the mm-th probabilist Hermite polynomial, which is the standard polynomial choice under our choice of data measure, and w∗∈ℝSw_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{S} is some normalized vector. The networks are trained via Lengevin dynamics welling_bayesian_nodate, with ridge parameter κ\kappa, quadratic weight decay, and standard scaling. For an extension to mean-field scaling, see App. E.1.1.

E.1.1 Fully Connected Networks

Standard scaling.

We turn to compute E~q\tilde{E}_{q} for a range of feature learning patterns. For this shallow FCN (and Nw=1N_{w}=1), our choice of feature learning patterns amounts to considering distributions in a single layer. We consider the following three scenarios (though more combinations are possible): (1) all neurons are GP distributed, (2) all are GFL distributed with amplification DD, and (3) MM neurons specialize on a the same feature, while those remaining are GP distributed. As the kernel of the first layer can only express linear features, the only relevant feature to be considered for the GFL and M-specialization patterns is Φ∗​(x)=w∗⋅x\Phi_{*}(x)=w_{*}\cdot x. We compute the scale of the optimal variational energy for each pattern:

  1. (1)

    GP: Here, Δ1,i=0\Delta_{1,i}=0 since Kl−1=QlK_{l-1}=Q_{l}. In this baseline setting, learning m>1m>1 is hard since ⟨H​em|K2|H​em⟩=𝒪⁡(d−m)\langle He_{m}|K_{2}|He_{m}\rangle=\mathcal{O}(d^{-m}) (see Sec. 5.2). Thus, in total, we have E~q∼GP∝dm\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GP}}\propto d^{m}.

  2. (2)

    GFL: Following (11), this pattern incurs a cost of Δ1,i=D\Delta_{1,i}=D per neuron ii, resulting in a total cost of N​DND. The aya_{y} term can be calculated utilizing Claim (ii). This leads to a DmD^{m}-factor decrease in the RKHS norm relative to the GP, so that ay∝(d/D)ma_{y}\propto(d/D)^{m}. In total, we find that E~q∼GFL∝N​D+(d/D)m\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GFL}}\propto ND+(d/D)^{m}. Minimizing w.r.t. DD, we obtain Dmin=(dm/N)1/(m+1)D_{\min}=(d^{m}/N)^{1/(m+1)}, and, substituting back, we obtain E~q∼GFL∝(N​d)mm+1\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GFL}}\propto(Nd)^{\frac{m}{m+1}}.

  3. (3)

    M-Specialization: Following 11, this pattern incurs a cost of Δ1=M⁡⟨Φ∗,K0−1​Φ∗⟩=M​d\Delta_{1}=M\langle\Phi_{*},K_{0}^{-1}\Phi_{*}\rangle=Md, where we denote Δl=∑iΔl,i\Delta_{l}=\sum_{i}\Delta_{l,i}. Utilizing Claim (i), this results in adding a spike with an M/NM/N coefficient along σ⁡(w∗⋅x)\sigma(w_{*}\cdot x) in K1K_{1} appearing in aya_{y}. Before this spike, H​em​(x)He_{m}(x) only had overlaps with the mm-th order Taylor expansion of the kernel, leading to a d−md^{-m} scaling. However, since σ⁡(w∗⋅x)\sigma(w_{*}\cdot x) has an 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) overlap with H​em​(x)He_{m}(x), so that ay∝N/Ma_{y}\propto N/M, we obtain E~q∼M-Sp∝d​M+N/M\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}\propto dM+N/M. Minimizing further over MM, the number of specializing neurons leads to Mmin=N/dM_{\min}=\sqrt{N/d} and therefore E~q∼M-Sp∝d​N\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}\propto\sqrt{dN}.

Now, we can compare the different feature learning patterns. Taking the most common linear scaling where N∝dN\propto d, the specialization scenario has the lowest variational energy. Our scaling theory then predicts an 𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(d) sample complexity as well as multimodal distribution of ww along w∗w_{*} with 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) specializing neurons. Taking m>1m>1 and N≫d5N\gg d^{5}, lazy learning wins and leads to 𝒪⁡(dm)\mathcal{O}(d^{m}) complexity. When m=1m=1, GFL and M-specialization are on par for N∝dN\propto d. These calculations coincide with both experimental and direct LDT results, as demonstrated in Fig. 2 for networks trained on H​e3He_{3}. In terms of sample complexity, both predictions agree with experiment, with a scaling of P∗∝dP_{*}\propto d, as seen in Fig. 2 (b). Our heuristic approach correctly predicts the scaling of the number of specializing neurons with NN, as seen in Fig. 2 (c). Finally, as shown in panel (a), the analytical LDT method recovers the correct pre-activation distribution, which corresponds to q⁡(h)q(h) for q∼M-Spq\sim\text{M-Sp}.

Extension to Mean-field Scaling

Here we extend the results presented in the main text to the case of mean-field scaling. We note that the results presented for standard scaling can change when introducing mean-field parametrization, amounting here to enhancing the alignment factor by a χ=𝒪⁡(N)\chi=\mathcal{O}(N) factor. The GP pattern then results in a much worse energy E~G​P=N​d3\tilde{E}_{GP}=Nd^{3}. Revisiting the GFL pattern, we now find E~G​F​L=N​D+N​(d/D)m\tilde{E}_{GFL}=ND+N(d/D)^{m} leading to D∝d1/(m+1)D\propto d^{1/(m+1)} and E~G​F​L,o​p​t​i​m​a​l∝N​dm/(m+1)\tilde{E}_{GFL,optimal}\propto Nd^{m/(m+1)}. For specialization, we obtain E~s​p=d​M+N2/M\tilde{E}_{sp}=dM+N^{2}/M, leading to M∝N/dM\propto N/\sqrt{d} and E~s​p,o​p​t​i​m​a​l∝d​N\tilde{E}_{sp,optimal}\propto\sqrt{d}N. Taking N∝dN\propto d, the specialization scenario again wins over for m>1m>1, with a sub-extensive (𝒪⁡(d)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d})) number of specializing neurons. Unlike with standard-parametrization, we see that even when taking N→∞N\rightarrow\infty, we remain in the rich regime. However, at least in this Bayesian finite-ridge setting, sample complexity is better with standard parametrization.

E.1.2 CNNs with Non-overlapping Patches.

Our approach can be extended to CNNs as defined by the following equation

f⁡(x)=∑i=1Nw∑j=1Nwi​j(2)​σ​(wj(1)⋅xi),f(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}w^{(2)}_{ij}\,\sigma(w^{(1)}_{j}\cdot x_{i}), (79)

with Nw>1N_{w}>1. In this case, it is better to focus on the covariance of wiw_{i}, namely, Σ=N−1​∑i=1Nwi​wiT\Sigma=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}w^{T}_{i}, than on the covariance of pre-activations on each path. One can then show that the cost becomes Δ1=Eqw​w⊤​[Σ−1−IS/S]​w\Delta_{1}={\rm E}_{q_{w}}w^{\top}\left[\Sigma^{-1}-I_{S}/S\right]w.

  1. (1)

    GP: In this scenario, the output kernel is given by K2,CNN​(x,x′)=Nw−1​∑i=1NwK2,FCN​(xi,xi′)K_{2,\text{CNN}}(x,x^{\prime})=N_{w}^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}K_{2,\text{FCN}}(x_{i},x_{i}^{\prime}), where K2,FCNK_{2,\text{FCN}} is the FCN kernel (Nw=1N_{w}=1). Focusing on a linear target for simplicity, we can work out the scaling of the relevant (linear) kernel feature by Taylor expanding K2,FCN=a1​xi⋅xi′/SK_{2,\text{FCN}}=a_{1}x_{i}\cdot x^{\prime}_{i}/S to get K2,CNN=a1Nw​S​x⋅x′K_{2,\text{CNN}}=\frac{a_{1}}{N_{w}S}x\cdot x^{\prime}, with a1a_{1} being some 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) constant. Lazy learning then yields E~q∼GP=Nw​S=d\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GP}}=N_{w}S=d, as in a FCN with no weight sharing.

  2. (2)

    GFL: Here, we take Σ=IS/S+D​w∗​w∗⊤\Sigma=I_{S}/S+Dw_{*}w_{*}^{\top}, resulting in Δl=1=N​D\Delta_{l=1}=ND. The leading term of the Taylor expansion now equals K2,CNN=1Nw​S​∑i=1Nwxi⊤​Σ​xi′K_{2,\text{CNN}}=\frac{1}{N_{w}S}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{w}}x_{i}^{\top}\Sigma x^{\prime}_{i} leading to a D/(Nw​S)D/(N_{w}S) scaling of the target. All in all, we find that E~q∼GFL=N​D+(Nw​S)/D\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GFL}}=ND+(N_{w}S)/D, leading to E~q∗=N​Mw​S\tilde{E}_{q_{*}}=\sqrt{NM_{w}S} for the optimal q∗∼GFLq_{*}\sim\text{GFL}.

  3. (3)

    M-Specialization: In this case, we obtain a Δl=1=M​S\Delta_{l=1}=MS cost. The contribution of the MM specializing neurons to the kernel goes as a1​MNw​N​∑i=1(w∗⋅x)​(w∗⋅x′)\frac{a_{1}M}{N_{w}N}\sum_{i=1}(w_{*}\cdot x)(w_{*}\cdot x^{\prime}), leading to ay=⟨y,KL,y⟩=𝒪⁡(M/Nw​N)a_{y}=\langle y,K_{L},y\rangle=\mathcal{O}(M/N_{w}N). Thus, E~q∼M-Sp=M​S+Nw​N/M\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}=MS+N_{w}N/M resulting in the optimal variational energy S​Nw​N\sqrt{SN_{w}N}.

Both GFL and M-Specialization patterns, in the proportionate limit N∝Nw∝S→∞N\propto N_{w}\propto S\rightarrow\infty, lead to P∗∝S3/2=d3/4P_{*}\propto S^{3/2}=d^{3/4}. This recovers results reported in ringel_applications_2025 computed via a mean-field approach.

E.2 Classification Tasks

We consider a fully connected network as defined in  78 with Nw=1N_{w}=1 and ReLU activations, trained on a kk-parity classification task. Explicitly, this task is defined as-

yk​(x)=sign​∏j=1kxj,y_{k}(x)=\text{sign}\prod_{j=1}^{k}x_{j}, (80)

where η∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), and for i=1,..,di=1,..,d, xi=si+𝒩⁡(0,ϵ)x_{i}=s_{i}+\mathcal{N}(0,\epsilon), for and sis_{i} that are i.i.d. random binary valuables in {±1}\{\pm 1\}. We take cross-entropy loss, and consider k=2k=2.

Here we observe that the target is given by-

y2​(x)=sign​((x1+η1)​(x2+η2))=sign​(12​(x1+x2)2−x12−x22)y_{2}(x)=\text{sign}((x_{1}+\eta_{1})(x_{2}+\eta_{2}))=\text{sign}(\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}+x_{2})^{2}-x_{1}^{2}-x_{2}^{2}) (81)

This setting is similar to the previously discussed polynomial target in the erf networks. The difference in this case is that there are multiple relevant directions, namely: w∗,1=e^1,w∗,2=e^2,w∗,1+2=e^1+e^2w_{*,1}=\hat{e}_{1},w_{*,2}=\hat{e}_{2},w_{*,1+2}=\hat{e}_{1}+\hat{e}_{2}, and up to multiplicative constants on the target and constant additions. As in the previous cases, we compute the scale of the optimal variational energy for each pattern, and consider the same patterns as in the two layer network. In this case, we can further consider another setting of feature learning. Rather than taking MM specializing neurons, and setting each of them to specialize with amplitude μ=1\mu=1, we can set ≈1\approx 1 neuron to specialize with magnitude μ\mu. As the erf was a bounded activation, this choice was not beneficial in that case we did not need to consider it as well. Defining the last pattern as μ\mu-Specialization, and comparing to the previously discussed patterns, we obtain:

  1. (1)

    GP: Here, Δ1,i=0\Delta_{1,i}=0 since Kl−1=QlK_{l-1}=Q_{l}. As in the case of the erf network, we have E~q∼GP∝d2\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GP}}\propto d^{2}.

  2. (2)

    GFL: Here we have E~q∼GFL∝N​D+(d/D)2\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GFL}}\propto ND+(d/D)^{2}. Minimizing w.r.t. DD, we obtain Dmin=d2/3/N1/3D_{\min}=d^{2/3}/N^{1/3}, and, substituting back, we obtain E~q∼GFL∝(N​d)23\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{GFL}}\propto(Nd)^{\frac{2}{3}}.

  3. (3)

    M-Specialization: E~q∼M-Sp∝d​M+N/M\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}\propto dM+N/M. Minimizing further over MM, the number of specializing neurons leads to Mmin=N/dM_{\min}=\sqrt{N/d} and therefore E~q∼M-Sp∝d​N\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}\propto\sqrt{dN}.

  4. (4)

    μ\mu-Specialization: Following 11, and the second feature propagation rule, we obtain this pattern incurs a cost of Δ1=μ2​d\Delta_{1}=\mu^{2}d. Utilizing the first feature propagation rule, this pattern results in adding a spike of the kernel so that ay∝N/μ2a_{y}\propto N/{\mu^{2}}, we obtain E~q∼M-Sp∝d​μ2+N/μ2\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{M-Sp}}\propto d\mu^{2}+N/\mu^{2}. Minimizing further over μ\mu, the magnitude of the specializing neurons leads to μmin=(N/d)1/4\mu_{\min}=(N/d)^{1/4} and therefore E~q∼μ-Sp∝d​N\tilde{E}_{q\sim\text{$\mu$-Sp}}\propto\sqrt{dN}.

There is a redundancy in the preferential patterns, as both specialization distributions result in a variational energy that scales as P∗∝N​dP_{*}\propto\sqrt{Nd}. Experimentally, we find that indeed the feature learning patterns that emerge for this case correspond to μ\mu-Specialization, with the correct scaling of the specialization magnitude with the layer width, as can be seen in  7.

E.3 Softmax Attention Layer

Here, we consider an attention block of the form

f⁡(X)\displaystyle f(X) =1L​∑h=1H∑a,b=1L@a​b;h​(X)​(wh⋅xb)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{a,b=1}^{L}@_{ab;h}(X)(w_{h}\cdot x^{b}) (82)
@a​b;h​(X)\displaystyle@_{ab;h}(X) =e[xa]⊤​Ah​xb∑c=1Le[xa]⊤​Ah​xc\displaystyle=\frac{e^{[x^{a}]^{\top}A_{h}x^{b}}}{\sum_{c=1}^{L}e^{[x^{a}]^{\top}A_{h}x^{c}}}

where X∈ℝL×d,Ah∈ℝd×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d},A_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, xa∈ℝdx^{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the aa-th row of XX, and wh∈ℝdw_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Our prior over network weights is ∏h=1H𝒩⁡[0,Id2/d2;Ah]​𝒩​[0,Id/(d​H);wh]\prod_{h=1}^{H}{\cal N}[0,I_{d^{2}}/d^{2};A_{h}]{\cal N}[0,I_{d}/(dH);w_{h}]. The only context length (LL) dependence comes from the pre-factor of 1/L1/\sqrt{L} which ensures that when Xia∼𝒩⁡(0,1)X^{a}_{i}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,1) then we have f⁡(X)=𝒪⁡(1)f(X)=\mathcal{O}(1). We consider the target function y⁡(X)=∑a,b1L⁡(L−1)​x1a​x2b​x3by(X)=\sum_{a,b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{L(L-1)}}x^{a}_{1}x^{b}_{2}x^{b}_{3}.

As H→∞H\rightarrow\infty, the above f⁡(X)f(X) tends to a GP with whw_{h} taking the role of read-out layer weights and a kernel given by

K⁡(X,X′)\displaystyle K(X,X^{\prime}) =(d​L)−1​∑a,a′,b,b′=1L(xb⋅(x′)b′)​𝔼A​[@a​b​(X)​@a′​b′​(X′)],\displaystyle=(dL)^{-1}\sum_{a,a^{\prime},b,b^{\prime}=1}^{L}(x^{b}\cdot(x^{\prime})^{b^{\prime}})\mathbb{E}_{A}\left[@_{ab}(X)@_{a^{\prime}b^{\prime}}(X^{\prime})\right], (83)

where we dropped the multi-head index hh by our i.i.d. assumption.

Our goal is to find the sample complexity and scaling of feature learning effects with context length (LL) at finite dd. To this end, we shall consider the following weight-space version of E~\tilde{E} given by,

E~q\displaystyle\tilde{E}_{q} =∑h=1Hd2​𝔼Ah∼qh​[T​r​[Ah​Ah⊤]−1]+1⟨y,K,y⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{h=1}^{H}d^{2}\mathbb{E}_{A_{h}\sim q_{h}}\left[Tr[A_{h}A_{h}^{\top}]-1\right]+\frac{1}{\langle y,K,y\rangle}. (84)

where KK is computed using the qhq_{h} distribution for AA. There are several ways of obtaining this variational energy; a direct microscopic route is shown in Sec. E.3.1. Alternatively, one can use the arguments of Sec. D, previously employed in Sec. E.1.2, and trade the kernel version of Δl,i\Delta_{l,i} with the excess weight decay of that layer. The latter being the first term in the above formula.

We will focus on two learning patterns here: lazy learning (GP) and weight specialization. For lazy learning, we take qh=𝒩⁡[0,Id2×d2/d2;Ah]q_{h}={\cal N}[0,I_{d^{2}\times d^{2}}/d^{2};A_{h}] leading, as expected, to zero contribution from the first term in E~q\tilde{E}_{q}.

E.3.1 Direct derivation of E~q\tilde{E}_{q} for a softmax block

Gathering all Ah,wA_{h},w parameters into Θ\Theta, the probability of aligment α\alpha is given by

Appendix F Experimental details

F.0.1 Two-layer FCN- Experimental Details

In panels (a) and (b) of Fig. 2, the experimental data points were computed by training an ensemble of 300 networks. For panel (a), all experiments used P=40​dP=40d and N=d=40N=d=40, with a ridge parameter of 11 and variances of σ12=σ22=1\sigma_{1}^{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}=1. For panel (b), we set N=dN=d while varying both dd and PP. The experimental value of P∗P_{*} was calculated by extrapolating from the different values of PP and their corresponding alignments, and then inverting this correspondence to find the value of PP for which Af=0.1A_{f}=0.1.

In panel (c), we set P=40​dP=40d and d=40d=40, while increasing the value of NN. As in the other panels, we used σ12=σ22=1\sigma_{1}^{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}=1, but here we set the ridge parameter to κ=0.25\kappa=0.25. We trained an ensemble of 300 networks and computed a histogram of the pre-activation alignment in the hidden layer. First-layer outliers were defined as any pre-activations having an overlap with Φ∗​(x)=w∗⋅x\Phi_{*}(x)=w_{*}\cdot x of more than 3​σ1/d3\sigma_{1}/\sqrt{d} (three times the standard deviation of the GP distribution). The total number of such outliers was counted and then averaged over the ensemble of networks.

F.1 Three-layer FCN- Experimental Details

In panel (a) of Fig. 3, the experimental data was computed by training an ensemble of 30 networks. For all experiments, we set d=N1=N2d=N_{1}=N_{2}, with a ridge parameter of 0.1250.125 and variances of σ12=σ22=0.25\sigma_{1}^{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}=0.25.

For panel (c) of Fig. 3 and in Fig. 8, we set P=40​dP=40d and d=N2=10d=N_{2}=10, while increasing the value of N1N_{1}. We further used σ12=σ22=0.25\sigma_{1}^{2}=\sigma_{2}^{2}=0.25 and a ridge parameter of κ=0.125\kappa=0.125. An ensemble of 300 networks was trained to compute the following histograms for the pre-activation alignments: 1. of the linear feature in the first hidden layer, 2. with the linear feature in the second layer, and 3. with the target in the second layer. Outliers in the first layer were calculated as in the two-layer case. For the second layer, activation alignments deviating by more than 3 times the NNGP standard deviation were considered outliers.

F.2 Alignment as a tight bound on MSE

A central component of our approach is using alignment as a certificate for good learning. As discussed in the main body of the text, the alignment is indeed a lower bound on the MSE through the inequality MSE≥(1−Af)2\geq(1-A_{f})^{2}. However, this inequality does not necessitate that the MSE will vanish. We therefore provide in this section empirical evidence that strong alignment is indeed an indication of MSE. To this extent, we provide results both from the softmax attention experiments and the three layer case, and in both we find that strong alignment is closely correlated with low loss, as can be seen in Fig.

Appendix G Comparing Kernel Adaptation and LDT

The results in the heuristic approach presented here are closely related to the kernel adaptation approach fischer_critical_2024, seroussi_separation_2023, ringel_applications_2025, rubin_grokking_2024, rubin_kernels_2025. In this section, we compute explicitly the mean posterior predictor for the alignment. Interestingly, we find that the equations for the LDT approach are remarkably similar to those of the mean predictor.

As in the derivation of the Chernhof bounds we begin by integrating out the readout weights from the posterior, and introducing a delta function Fourier field in the prior, we obtain-

where t~\tilde{t} is an imaginary helper field originating from the delta function. Define-
